REFERENCE OF ANNUAL REPORTS AND CERTAIN E6TIMATES TO RAILWAYS AND SHIPPING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to lay on the table the following reports in English and in French: annual report of the Canadian National Railway system for the year ended December 31, 1946; annual report of the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited for the year ended December 31, 1946; annual report of the Canadian National Securities Trust for the year ended December 31, 1946. Copies of these reports are being distributed to hon. members this afternoon. The auditors' report to parliament has been delayed in printing but I am informed that the English edition will be ready for tabling Thursday next and the French edition a day or two later.
By leave of the house I move:
That the annual reports for 1946 of the Canadian National Railway system, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited and the Canadian National Securities Trust tabled this day be referred to the sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government, together with the following items of the estimates for 1947-48:
Vote 434. Maritime Freight Rates Act, Canadian National Railways;
Vote 435. Maritime Freight Rates Act, railways other than Canadian National;
Vote 479. Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals deficit, 1947.
And that the resolution passed by the house on March 4, 1947, referring certain estimates to the committee of supply, be rescinded in so far as the said resolution relates to votes Nos. 434, 435 and 479.
Motion agreed to.

Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I shall be glad to send a copy of the report to my hon. friend. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There are a few questions I should like to ask in regard to this particular item, which has to do with the setting up of a corporation for the purpose of continuing the control over sugar. As the committee is aware, oni March 31 the United1 States passed an order continuing sugar control and rationing until October 31, 1947, at which time, as was indicated when this extension was made, sugar control will come to an end in the United States. Today each country in the international pool receives an alio-

Emergency Powers
cation of sugar under an international agreement. When President Truman signed) the bill extending sugar control he saidl this:
While our supplies-
He was referring to the supplies in the United States of America.

in 1947 will be larger than those available last year, they will still be substantially below pre-war per capita supply and still further below estimated demands ... A premature ending of controls over sugar would bring about a scramble of competing countries for the inadequate supplies now in prospect.
Canada gets 82 per cent of her yearly sugar supplies from foreign sources. In a return which was brought down last month it was revealed that 47 per cent of Canada's sugar supplies came from the British West Indies and Fiji, 35 per cent from non-empire countries, and only 18 per cent from her own domestic beet sugar production. How is it that in spite of the opportunities which are ours, with our refining facilities, no real encouragement is given to sugar beet production? The six beet sugar plants have a maximum capacity of 150,000 tons of refined sugar, which is 26 per cent of Canada's 1946 allocation, and is 44 per cent higher than the goal set by the government this year. Some might say, "Well, what advantage would there be?- because Canada receives only a proportionate share of the world's sugar supply under international agreement." I suggest that if further encouragement were given by the federal government to sugar beet production in this country it would mean two things. For one thing, increased1 production-and I am informed that it could run about 50 per cent higher than the present figure-would mean a larger international pool, thereby assuring Canadian consumers of a larger share of sugar. It would also make available a wider distribution in the countries of Europe which require sugar.
I know there has been a change this year. One dollar per hundredweight increase in price has been allowed, and the government grants a 25 cent subsidy, but that is no additional encouragement. All that the government has done has been to pass on to the consumer the extra amount of one cent per pound; there has been no additional encouragement this year to the producer in this country to produce to the limit of the capacity available. For some reason it seems impossible to get consideration of the problem from those in charge of this corporation. Their attitude is that sugar is not a crop indigenous to Canada, if I might use that expression. But, sir, in Manitoba and in Alberta it is being widely extended; and in my own province of Saskat-83166-140
chewan there is an area in the Qu'Appelle valley peculiarly fitted by nature and the contour of the land to produce sugar beets and practically nothing else. I should like the minister to make a statement as to the government's attitude with regard to the encouragement and expansion of sugar beet production, so that this crop, which has become a kind of insurance crop wherever it is produced, may be extended in acreage and amount, to the end that there will be improvement in the opportunities for production and a larger quota available to consumers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in answer to my hon. friend. Pre-war beet sugar production was about 150 million pounds annually. The maximum production of beet sugar in Canada was in the year 1940, production for that year being 213 million pounds. Production in 1946 was 207 million pounds. The capacity of the factories in Canada is 300 million pounds. .
It is not correct to say that no encouragement has been given to the production of beet sugar in Canada. In 1946 a subsidy of 604 cents per hundred pounds was paid. In 1947 that figure was increased to $1.25, of which 25 cents is now in the form of a subsidy and $1 in the form of increased price. As the hon. member has said, we in. this country produce 18 per cent of our requirements at home. It is possible that by paying enough money in subsidies or by raising our tariffs high enough we could increase the production in Canada under peacetime conditions to considerably more than 18 per cent of our total consumption. A matter of policy comes in there, as to how intense a degree of protectionism, because that is what it is, we should apply to the production of beet sugar. That production can be increased, as I say, by the payment of enough money eitheT by the taxpayers or the consumers; by the taxpayers in the way of subsidies or by the consumers in the way of prices. But a balance of some kind must be struck there, and a reasonable course taken. I do not know what my hon. friend would suggest. He must hold, the same position, I should think, that a moderate course must be taken between the two extremes, because I do not think he would take the highly protectionist position that we should put our prices so high, our tariffs so high, our subsidies so high, that we would produce, in Canada all the sugar we required, and exclude sugar from empire sources, particularly at a time when we are greatly in need of imports from empire sources in order to create dollars with which to make markets for ourselves abroad.
The policy of the government has been a reasonable one. We have not discriminated in

Emergency Powers

any way against the beet sugar industry in Canada. The production figures I have given are. reasonable. The hon. member for Stan-stead saidi one of the great factories in southwestern Ontario is idle but the prime factor in that situation was lack of labour, and I understand prospects are that both factories will be operating there, with an improvement in production. The contracts signed in the last ten days have been greater than ever before in the history of the beet sugar growing area.
The suggestion has been made that if we had forced to a greater extent the growing of sugar beets in Canada, we would have increased the amount of sugar available for our consumers. AVell, we get about six per cent of the world production of sugar, or the production that is available for Great Britain, the United States and Canada. To the extent that we increased production in Canada that would go into the pool under the international allocation arrangements and out of the pool we would get six per cent of the increase, which would not be very much. It is just a question how much of the money of the taxpayers or how much of the money of the consumers we would be justified in paying in order to force that result. I think the course we have taken has been reasonable.

speechtext:
During the Easter vacation I was at a meeting of sugar beet growers in the city of Portage la Prairie. Representatives were .there endeavouring to get the sugar beet growers to sign contracts for another year. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I think it is a fact that the sugar beet producers of this country are held down in the price they get, because the price for their product is not allowed to equal the price for sugar made from imported sugar cane. You do not need to raise the tariff in order to get a greater production of sugar in Canada, certainly not in Manitoba. The sugar beet growers have been down here at least four times since last December trying to get. some satisfaction from the administrator. Finally I understand they had a conference with the Minister of Finance at which the last adjustment just mentioned by the Minister of Justice was arrived at. At every meeting of growers that I attend at which there are representatives of the association there is criticism of the present sugar administrator. I should like to know what will be his position in the future. Are we going to have the same sugar administrator? He does not have the confidence of the growers, who do not think he is giving them a fair deal as compared to cane sugar. The government must know that
IMr. Ilsley.l
from the comments of the delegations of growers every time they come down here. The growers are being urged to produce more, and the factories are trying to get contracts. At the factory of the Manitoba Sugar Beet Company on the Red river they want to get production up to 150,000 tons, as compared to their present maximum of 90,000. If the price paid the sugar beet growers was brought up to equality -with what is paid for cane sugar it seems to me you would have no difficulty getting more sugar beets produced, and consequently more sugar. Before I sit down I would like to know from the minister just w-hat is to be the position of the present sugar administrator under the new set-up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
I know that there is

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Well, to be valid, criticism has to be based upon facts, not upon what a man may have done previously in his lifetime, or something of that kind. Mr. Noble was a high official of the Royal Bank, which had some branches in Cuba and I believe at one time had some interest in cane sugar plantations. That was the fact upon which the whole criticism of Mr. Noble was based; but that is not sufficient. If criticism of a man is going to be made, for it to be valid you must put your finger on some facts. I am convinced that Mr. Noble has been scrupulously fair in his treatment of the beet sugar growers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I remind the minister that after the first war it was proved quite conclusively that some of the bank gentlemen who were mixed up with sugar did not'know very much about it; they were out about $16,000,000. so it is no recommendation to say that a man worked in a bank.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am not going to weary the minister with my views on subsidies; he knows them very well, but I should like to

Emergency Powers
ask if he does not consider that the method of applying the sugar subsidy has resulted in a curtailment of production in southwestern Ontario, as distinguished from other areas in which the growing of sugar beets was carried on during the war. The total production is about, on a level with what it was before the war, but in the great sugar beet area of southwestern Ontario production has decreased, whereas in Manitoba, Alberta and to some extent in Saskatchewan production has increased. Is it not a fact that the method of applying the subsidy has brought about this result? I am leaving aside the question of labour, because if I have correctly understood the situation the matter of labour has not been the determining factor in the abandoning by the farmers of southwestern Ontario of the cultivation of sugar beets.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The fact that competing products were subsidized at all probably did mean that a larger acreage was devoted to competing products than to sugar. But all the acreage was used; and there were years when it was thought better to produce beans, tomatoes, and the like, than to produce sugar. That was not fully carried out, of course, but it was thought desirable to increase the production of some of these products, which used land that otherwise might have been used for sugar. That was a matter of nutrition, a matter of getting production of the proper foods. If sugar had been subsidized and the others had not been, probably there would have been a larger acreage of sugar, despite the labour situation. But the matter of labour was a serious one in that district of Canada, because it is contiguous to the large industrial areas in which high wages were being paid, and where it was difficult to get labour.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not going to question the judgment of the government or of the department in subsidizing other products, which may have made it attractive to farmers in southwestern Ontario to grow those products in place of sugar beets. But is it not a fact that, in the result, the farmer growing sugar beets in Manitoba, or any of the prairie provinces, received a better price per ton for his beets than did the farmer in southwestern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He did, on account of the fact that he enjoys freight protection.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am aware of that. Again, I am not criticizing the government, but I am endeavouring to point out that the subsidy did not work out equally everywhere. The farmer in western Canada-and by that I mean Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta 83166-1463
-was getting from 75 cents to something over a dollar more per ton for his beets than was the farmer in southwestern Ontario. That was a considerable incentive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The same rate of subsidy was paid everywhere. The price was higher in the west. They are entitled to a higher price because of the freight.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The point I wish to make is that southwestern Ontario, being the area par excellence in which the sugar beet can be produced, where the industry was firmly established, and where the people were acquainted with all the methods of good production, should have been treated differently. It seems to me that the growth of sugar beets could have been stimulated there to better advantage than by opening up new areas in which the whole population had to be taught the industry from the beginning. I shall not say poor judgment was used, but I shall say the government could have got a larger quantity of sugar with less effort from southwestern Ontario than from the new area, in which as it were it started the growth and development of a new sugar beet industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think the comparison between Ontario and Alberta holds. I believe Alberta is placed just as favourably, and perhaps more favourably, in the production of sugar beets.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In connection with the minister's statement to the effect that encouragement to the industry-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would speak louder. I am interested, in what he is saying, but down here we can hear nothing but a whisper.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The interruption supports the suggestion made by the hon. member for Fort William, that loud speakers-be installed in the chamber, should have been: carried into effect. I am waiting for the improved suggestion in that regard which he said would be forthcoming shortly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minister stated that if any further encouragement were given to sugar beet production it would not mean any additional ration to the consumers, because under the international agreement Canada is entitled to only six per cent of the available supply. Theoretically that is true. But in the United States, when President Truman made the announcement to which I
Emergency Powers

referred a few minutes ago, he said that a portion of the increase in the production of beet sugar would be passed on to the consumer, and that the consumer would be entitled to a sugar ration in the coming year larger than he would be entitled to under the proportionate share of the United States by virtue of the international agreement.
Today in the United States the ration share is 35 pounds per capita. That is the quota for householders in that country. Under the new plan enunciated by the President, and through encouragement given to sugar beet production, an extra ration to the extent of 15 pounds per individual will be passed on to the consumer. In other words, while under the international agreement the present quota is 35 pounds, if the sugar beet production of the United States is increased to the extent of 15 pounds per capita, that increase will be passed on to the consumer. While it is true the subsidy of 25 cents and the additional price of a dollar a hundredweight does afford some advantage to the producer, I suggest that the sugar beet production about which the minister spoke in such glowing terms would not have taken place in Ontario, had it not been for the subsidy of $112,500 granted by the Ontario government, which is to be made available this year to sugar beet producers. If, under rthe international agreement, the United .'States is in a position to add to the ration that the consumer will receive through Increased beet sugar production, is there any reason why Canada should be in any different position?
My second point is that if encouragement is given to sugar beet production in Canada, and Canada continues to be restricted to six per cent of the international output, we would be conserving United States dollars which, if the exchange situation is as it is described in the press, is so necessary today. The amount invested in the course of the year in importing sugar into this country is some $23,000,000, U.S. funds, and that is very necessary to our international financial set-up. If we produced that sugar in Canada we would be saving that money as well as giving encouragement to the producers and providing a kind of insurance for agricultural production. Canada is producing more sugar beets today than heretofore; is there any reason why we could not extend the rationing, as has been done in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We have increased our ration of sugar along with the United States.
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have suggested that by reason of the increased production of sugar beets ration amounts could be increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know how long this international allocation will continue and I assume my hon. friend is talking more about a long term policy than one for the next twelve months or so. I am told it is expected that the beet sugar production in Canada will reach an all-time high in 1947. It could be driven up further and the imports from empire countries-they are mainly from empire countries, certainly in time of peace- can be pressed down if we want to spend enough money to do it. But, as I said before, that is protectionism of the very highest type.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Under this government we have had the highest protection in the history of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not talking politics; I am talking about my hon. friend's proposal. It is not altogether desirable to crush out imports from the sterling area, and it is not altogether desirable to make different areas completely self-sufficient in everything. If you do that, you cut off international trade. I think the beet sugar growers should be treated fairly, and in my submission they have been treated fairly. They have not secured every subsidy that they applied for, and the same applies to every other group in Canada that has applied for a subsidy. So far as I know, their demands have not been fully met. When I was in the Department of Finance we received delegations and we turned down requests for subsidies of much greater magnitude than those that were granted. Very often the subsidy granted was not as much as what was asked for, and the same applied to practically every other agricultural product. The requests made exceeded what was eventually done. I think those are the only points raised by my hon. friend.

speechtext: Before the war the plant capacity in southwestern Ontario was being operated to about one hundred per cent of its capacity, but according to the information I have it is being operated today only to the extent of sixty or sixty-five per cent. In order to give the proper background of this order in council it will be necessary for me to take some little time, but I shall give it if the hon. member wishes it. I know he is interested in this item.
The Pelagic Sealing Convention of 1911 entered into between Great Britain, United States, Japan and Russia respecting measures for the preservation and protection of the fur seals in the north Pacific ocean was ratified in Canada by the Pelagic Sealing (Convention) Act 1938. Chapter 17 of the act provided' that the act shall continue in force until a day which may be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council following upon the termination of the convention.
On the 24th of October, 1940 in pursuance of article 16 of the convention, a notice of abrogation was given by Japan, and in accordance with the provisions of the convention, it expired on the 23rd of October, 1941.
A provisional fur seal agreement was entered into between Canada and the United States by exchange of notes dated December 8, 1942 and December 19, 1942 covering a portion of the waters of the north Pacific ocean.
It was stipulated by article 10 of the provisional agreement that it would1 remain in effect for the duration of the present emergency and twelve months thereafter.
The provisional agreement between Canada and United States was confirmed in Canada by order in council P.C. 4112 of May 30, 1944 passed under the War Measures Act. This

Emergency Powers
order in, council likewise fixed) the tenth day of June, 1944 as the day for the expiry of the Pelagic Sealing (Convention) Act 1938, as provided for in section 17 of the said act.
On December 31, 1946 the President of the United States proclaimed that in so far as the United States was concerned the hostilities of world war II had terminated as of noon, December 31, 1946. As a result of this proclamation those portions of United States statutes respecting fur seals which specifically implement the 1942 provisional fur seal agreement between the United States and Canada, will cease to be effective at twelve o'clock noon December 31, 1947. The government of the United States is now considering an arrangement to replace the provisional fur seal agreement of 1942 and will communicate with the government of Canada at the earliest possible date with respect to such arrangement. In the meantime-and this is what my hon. friend wants to know-in order to keep in force the provisional fur seal agreement of 1942, the one we are working under, until December 31, 1947, it is necessary to continue in effect the present order in council P.C. 4112 of May 30, 1944.

This order in council has to do with prosecutions taken under part 15 of the criminal code and the right of appeal is provided in respect of infractions of wartime regulations. I appeal to the minister to communicate with the officials administering the wartime prices and trade board and to point out to them the necessity of proceeding with proper regard to the rights of the individual. During the war arbitrary actions on the part of those charged with the investigation and prosecution of offences against these regulations were more or less tolerated. Now in the days of peace, even though this legislation, be carried on for the time being, the rights of the individual must be assured.
I hold no brief on behalf of those who are deliberately breaking the law, but I suggest that the retail merchant or the honest business man who makes a momentary slip which constitutes a contravention of regulations, some of which he does not know of unless he is omniscient, should not be harassed. I shall not discuss in detail the cases I have in mind, but I suggest that in making investigations these officials should be instructed to use care. Particulars in support of my contention that frequently that is not done, I do not intend to place before the committee at this time, but I suggest that the minister ask the officials who are conducting investigations to use discretion, to warn people where a warning is possible, and to prosecute only where there is apparently a continuing intention to circumvent the law.
Some investigators arrogate to themselves the arbitrary power that characterizes many of those who exercise authority, however small or great. Some have developed a complex of harassing honest business men. I hope that will end and that the Minister of Justice will see that it does. Most of our people want to uphold the law, but on too many occasions the investigators proceed on the assumption that all the people want to break the law. That is a type of mind that can be easily
Emergency Powers

developed and it is the type of mind that has no place in a democracy. It leads to bureaucratic omnipotence and domination. Against that type of mind I make this protest, and I say this to the minister in no critical sense at all at the moment. If it is desired to enter into a critical argument I am prepared to do so, but I am putting this forward in a constructive way. I ask the minister to inform these officials that the Canadian people are law-abiding. The record of prosecutions shows that. Tell these men to use that discretion which an honest people have a right to demand of their officials.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the Minister of Justice will be better able to answer my first query, in any event. It is this. What is there in the industrial or labour-management situation in Canada today whereby any legislation with respect to that matter can possibly be justified by reason of an emergency? As far as I know the situation in Canada, with one exception is quieter in that field than it has been for a good many years. Personally I know of no reason in the world which would bring legislation extending certain orders in council under the heading of any emergency whatever. Perhaps I may pause for an answer there to help my ignorance, so to speak, and then I may be able to cut out a good deal of what I intended to say. I should like to know what the emergency is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not think the basis of this legislation is a separate emergency in respect of every particular measure. There being a state of emergency in existence as a result of war, an economic emergency; there having been this extraordinary legislation, P.C. 1003, during the wartime period, I think a reasonable period of readjustment to peacetime conditions must be allowed, during which the legislation should continue. This legislation is peculiarly short lived; it is just here until a bill can be introduced. The whole matter of adjustment of the economy from conditions of war to conditions of peace is the problem with respect to prices and wages and labour relations and all the other important aspects of the economic situation. As I said before, I do not think an emergency can be dissected. I do not think you can carve out segments and say there is an emergency in respect of this and not an emergency in respect of that, at least while you are in the economic field. There is not a military emergency; I hope there is not, and I think there is not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not intend to reopen the legal argument we had the other day, but surely from what the minister has now said his view is this. The dominion government can declare an emergency and then go into any field it wishes, just because it has said there is an emergency. That is what I gather from what the right hon. minister just said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, it is not a question of declaring an emergency. It is a question of there being an emergency; and when there is, it does not mean the government can go into any field it likes, but labour relations, the relations between employers and employees, are such an important feature of the economy of the country. If there are emergency con-
ditions affecting the economy of the country, if it is not readjusted to peace conditions then legislation on the matter of labour conditions can be enacted during that period.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Then it is just another step or two from there until the new bill is brought in. I think the minister will agree that when that bill is brought down it cannot take away from the provinces jurisdiction in matters of labour and industry. If that will be true in a couple of weeks from now, and I am sure the minister will agree it is true, there cannot be a state of emergency just to bridge this little gap. Would not the minister agree in that? Let me put it in this way. We are going to have a new so-called labour code brought in. Aside from the government or parliament assuming extraordinary power, to become an act that bill can do nothing more than legislate with respect to those persons now within the jurisdiction of the dominion government, and by "now" I mean in peace time; your transportation people, communications people, and so on. So that if we are going to have this bill brought into the house-and I noticed the Minister of Labour nodding his head in agreement a minute ago-then why clutter up this bill with the sort of thing we now have before us? Why do that, when we admit that in two weeks, we will say, we are going to bring down a labour code which shall be limited in its outlook and effect to those persons who come within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.
Why waste our time now in prolonging P.C. 1003-because that is what this legislation amounts to. I hope I make myself clear. I am simply trying to say this: Why do we not drop this thing altogether, and get on with something which may be of considerably more importance? There may be an answer to what I am saying, but I must say I have made some inquiry and I can find no answer.
Let me put it in this way, that if we did not pass this now jurisdiction would be back with the provinces immediately. It is going to be there in a couple of weeks, anyway, if we bring down our new legislation. I think the Minister of Labour will agree with me on that. And if the jurisdiction is to be with the provinces, then why not put it there now, and not waste our time in carrying on with this discussion.
I spoke on second reading, and one of the things I had in mind was that there were some things which should be done and some which ought not to be done. To my mind this is the biggest "ought not" of the lot. I can

Emergency Powers
see no virtue whatsoever in doing it. If there is no virtue in doing it, then I shall pause to be interrupted by someone who will tell me what it is. If there is virtue, then we can proceed with the discussion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I can answer the hon. member. What he says is correct. With the exception of railway matters, which come under the jurisdiction of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, in normal circumstances under our constitution wages and labour legislation are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. My hon. friend will recall that it was back in 1941 or 1942 it was felt, after consultation with the provinces, that in connection with our price policy we should establish a system of wage control.
I was the first chairman of the national war labour board, and it was my duty to get the provincial ministers of labour, or those ministers having jurisdiction over labour in the provinces, to meet here in Ottawa, on which occasion they agreed to withdraw from that control and to place it under the jurisdiction of the dominion. Those boards dealt specificalty with wages.
In the light of the growing tempo of the war, it was felt there should be a labour code governing the whole dominion, and the provinces again agreed.

I want to detain the committee for only a minute or two, if I am in order, to say something about the situation which exists at the present time in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and by that I mean the coal strike which has been going on for a few weeks, or for a considerable time in any event.
I have always held the belief that no labour disturbance can last any great length of time without some measure of public support. I have read all the literature which I am sure all hon. members have received from the united mine workers in Nova Scotia and the operating company. They seem to come to one simple statement on each side. It is a fact that tonnage has dropped to approximately a ton and a half per man, a drop of practically a full ton since 1939. The men say that they cannot do better because of working conditions and because of the failure to modernize certain machinery. On the other hand, the management say that the machinery is just as good as or better than it was in 1939. that conditions are comparable and that it is the men's fault.
The minister went through the various motions he was entitled to go through under our legislation and finally ended up by appointing Mr. Justice Carroll as a commissioner. But it does seem to me that there is one thing which has not been decided and which must have great effect on what the Department of Labour or any Minister of Labour may do. I refer to the determination of the simple question as to who is right Are the men right in saying that it is the fault of management, or is the management right in saying that it is the fault of the men because they will not work?
I do not want to be told to read the report of the royal commission on coal because not only have I read it, but I reread a portion of it when our father confessor over here on labour matters, the minister, told us to read it again. If the newspapers are to be believed, both the minister and his deputy have said that this is a matter in which the government is not interested, that it is purely a matter between management and men. If they were correctly quoted, both the minister and Mr. MacNamara made that statement. With that I respectfully but firmly disagree.
Year after year this parliament has voted some $8,000,000 as a subsidy to this operation and therefore it cannot be just a simple question between the management and the men. What, the minister is reported to have said would normally be correct in different places and under different conditions, but I urge that, while we are paying $8,000,000, we cannot just wash our hands of it and say that this is a question which can be settled by the other two parties. This is a three-party show because we are in it to the extent of $8,000,000. although this subsidy was eliminated just in the last week or two.

Mr. COLiDWELL: Mr. Chairman, the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary West is worthy of consideration, but I am not going to deal with it. One of the most striking indictments of conditions in that area of Canada was the statement made by the Minister of Labour a short time ago when he indicated the number of persons who had applied for work elsewhere than in Cape Breton and who were turned down on account of their physical unfitness. The number was simply phenomenal. It is a severe indictment of the conditions that have been prevalent in that area for a number of years. I do not think we should discuss the Nova Scotia mining problem at the moment; I think we should deal with it later at a more appropriate time.
I want to go back to the order in council. The Minister of Labour has indicated that he is going to bring down some new legislation. I wish to point out to him that we have evolved considerably from the conditions which existed in 1867, and the whole basis of legislative powers should be reexamined so that we may have a dominion code which will be applicable to labour from one end of this dominion to the other in

more fields than the narrow one outlined by the minister. I have been looking up important matters lately to see just how this order in council is in conformity with what existed in bygone days. If we look at our revised statutes of Canada we find that legislation dealing with trade unions is on our statute books, passed I believe, in 1872 and introduced in the house by Sir John A. Macdonald. Anyone who knows the story of confederation knows that Sir John A. Macdonald held strong views as to the necessity of matters of this description being more completely under the authority of the national government than under the provincial bodies. Going back into our history, we find that up until 1886 various pieces of legislation were introduced both in the House of Commons and in the Senate dealing with labour conditions in a much broader and wider way than apparently many are inclined to recognize as the right of this house in 1947.
A few minutes ago the Minister of Labour pleaded for the continuation of this order in council until his legislation is introduced. I submit that not only should we continue this order in council until his legislation comes down, but when that legislation is before us an endeavour should be made to clarify our powers in conformity with new conditions which face this country in 1947.
The other day I was looking over some material in connection with this order in council and this legislation. I am not going to weary the committee with anything like a constitutional argument because I am not a lawyer and I am not equipped to do so. Bather I wish to discuss the historic background. But as I said a few moments ago, bills were introduced in the house again and again by private members and, in some instances, by the government of the country. For example, in 1882 a bill was introduced in the senate by Sir Alexander Campbell who was a father of confederation, who was a partner of Sir John A. Macdonald and who was also Minister of Justice at that time. Sir Alexander Campbell insisted that the bill dealing with labour conditions across the country was in strict conformity with the powers of the dominion and with the intention of the fathers of confederation. The other day I took the trouble to look up a speech which he made in the senate on April 19, 1882, on the labour employment regulation bill, and I think it might be well to put parts of it on the record, in view of this order in council and in view of the legislation which is to be introduced later. He said:
The hon. member for Amherst, if I understand his argument right, thought this was a

Emergency Powers
matter that came wholly under the purview of the local legislatures, because it was a question of civil rights-of contracts between master and servant, hours of meals, and that sort of thing- and therefore belonged to the local legislatures, and that this bill did not come within the powers of parliament to pass it; but I venture to ask my hon. friend if that is not a very confined view of the bill? It is true that it does deal with the subject of contracts between master and servant, but is it not much more true, and true in a larger and better sense, that it relates to the welfare and well-being of the whole community?
And I mention that in 1947 this is more true of labour legislation. The hon. member for Calgary West has just indicated that a dispute in one province, largely in Nova Scotia, does affect the whole of our economy throughout the entire community which we call Canada.
Sir Alexander Campbell went on:
I listened with great pleasure to the arguments submitted to the house by the hon. senator from Prince Edward Island as to the effect upon the community of laxity with reference to the rules which this bill proposes to lay down. That hon. gentleman established, 1 think, to the satisfaction of the house that the result of the laxity of regulations or want of regulations, in this respect, in England, had a deteriorating effect upon the whole population who lived in the manufacturing districts. If that was the effect in England and if we are to presume that a similar one would follow the want of regulations and laxity of rules in this country, I ask if such an effect produced upon the whole population is not a very strong and even conclusive reason, why this parliament should deal with a question affecting the welfare and growth of the whole community, and the physical power and strength of those who form the nation? Surely if this subject relates to a question so generally important as that and which affects the whole country, it is a much larger one than if it related merely to contracts between master and servant. It is because this bill relates to subjects so important as that, subjects which go far beyond contracts between master and servant. which in their indirect effects concern the whole community and on which, to a certain extent, and so far as the population in manufacturing establishments go, the future of the country very much turns-whether we shall have a strong, healthy and moral population, likely to be creditable to the country or whether we shall have a dwarfed and immoral population and so perpetuate in Canada all the evils which this inquiry has brought out in England and which we are trying to legislate for now-* I say if these subjects do not affect the peace, order and welfare of a whole community it would be hard to say what does. Therefore, as they have that effect, the house, I hope and believe, will take a much larger view of the matter than has been presented, and which would confine this to a simple matter of interfering between master and servant. It is a much larger question: it is to provide for the future welfare, morality and good government of the whole community . . .
I think and hope that the arguments which I have presented to the house will show that this
bill is not merely for the purpose of interfering with contracts, but has a scope which is national in its character, and which may, and probably will be attended with the most useful results to those who are to come after us. Therefore it does come within the purview of the powers of this parliament, which it will be remembered has the right to deal with all questions affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, not specially assigned to the local legislatures.
Speaking of the two jurisdictions, that of the dominion and of the province, he says:
If the two conflict, and if it should be that it is both-and I think almost everybody in the house will say that it is both, that it is in a very narrow sense a question affecting civil rights and contracts, but that it is also in a much larger sense a national subject affecting the weal and good government of the people- if the two conflict, under the ordinary constitutional practice the lesser must give way, and we must legislate on the subject. To my mind, and to the best of my judgment, the house is quite seized with this measure, and it is within the powers of parliament to take what steps they deem in the interest of the country upon this question.
I think the time has come when we shall have to face up to the problem posed by order in council, to the situation when this order in council is removed from the statute books, and the question as to the necessary labour code which should follow. The important point I make is this. If we go back to the records we shall find that unfortunately the early speeches of the fathers of confederation in this house were not recorded in Hansard, and therefore all that one can do is to get summaries of them or to read, as best one can, some of the reports in newspapers of the day.

That was before 1882. I was about to say that when we come to the eighties we get actual verbatim reports such as we are used to now. I have not outlined the various labour bills that were introduced from time to time, either in this house or in the senate, during the time the fathers of confederation were members of parliament. But when the discussion to which I have referred took place a government bill was introduced in the senate by the then minister of justice, and therefore with the approval of the cabinet, and at that time there were, I believe, five fathers of confederation in the government. They were Sir John A. Macdonald, Tilley, Tupper, Langevin and Campbell himself. I know of some of the judgments that were given later on; I know the views of Lord Watson, and so on; but the point I make is that the fathers of confederation visualized this country as a nation

Emergency Powers
and not as a collection of more or less sovereign states. If you read the speeches and the writings of Sir John A. Macdonald you find that again and again he took the view that we were not doing something like that which some time before had been done in the United States but were doing something opposite to what they had done.
When I was teaching I used to read quite frequently the "Makers of Canada". This afternoon I recollected a statement to be found therein, I sent to the library and got a copy of volume X of the "Makers of Canada". I quote from page 59:
According to Macdonald, it was the aim of the fathers of the constitution to form a strong central government. "In framing the constitution, care had been taken to avoid the mistake and weakness of the United States system,' the primary error of which was the reservation to the different states of all the powers not delegated to the general government. We must reverse the process by establishing a strong central government, to which shall belong all powers not specially conferred on the provinces."
That was Sir John's idea at the beginning. I know Cartier disagreed with that point of view and a compromise was reached. No one wishes to upset the basis of confederation. No one wishes to set up so strong a central government that the provinces will have no jurisdiction in matters that are of provincial and local interest. But my point is that if the fathers of confederation, in matters of labour, as I believe they did, saw the need for nationwide legislation to meet nation-wide conditions in the field of labour, today, with our rapid means of communication, with the mobility of labour, and with all the new industries and methods which are nation-wide in scope, not only do we require an order in council like P.C. 1003 to be continued but we need dominion jurisdiction in a field where we must have dominion-wide conditions.
I am not arguing that we should take from the provinces something which is properly theirs. I am saying that in the interests of all Canada this parliament should have the power to legislate on matters that concern the whole country. During the war we had1 some of that power. It has been inherent in this order 1003. I wish to see P.C. 1003 continued until we have the legislation which the minister says he is bringing down, and I take this opportunity this afternoon, because I hope that when that legislation does come down the matters that properly belong to the province and the community shall remain to them, but that we shall hold fast to the original concept of a nation which, as I believe, the fathers of confederation had.
[Mr. Coldwell.)
I have done considerable reading on the confederation pact, and so on, and I know there was a compromise, but I think the time has come when in this important field of labour it is essential that we should have a nationwide concept of conditions and a nation-wide code which will establish for all Canada a proper basis of labour relations and conditions.

I rise to support the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. What he said this afternoon will have the support of organized labour in my constituency. As a member of parliament I am speaking for Canada, but I am speaking as one having some understanding of the outlook of organized labour in British Columbia and of many employers in British Columbia. At the present time we have industry organized largely in a national and international way, and we are dealing with organized labour which is largely organized in a national and international way. Gone are the horse and buggy days when we had the village industry just supplying local needs, the village shop and the limitations of transportation and communication. Today we are developing more and more into a large organization, as I said before, based on a national or international grouping, just as are the transportation companies, the packing companies, the mining interests, the lumbering interests and many other interests. Because of that the people whom I represent, and many others in western Canada, are anxious to see a national labour code established. I fully realize the constitutional difficulties which surround this question, particularly at this time, because there is no common agreement between the dominion and provincial governments in connection with, this and other legislation. But I do think this government should determine now the direction in which we are to go in the future in this respect. I think they should be bold because the need is urgent. I suggest that this government should bring in a national labour code, taking full cognizance of the development of industry and of society in general. If they cannot have that code accepted by all the provinces of Canada, by agreement, then I say it would be worth while to go ahead, introduce that code and have it accepted in those provinces that will accept it.
I am of opinion that it would not be very long before all the provinces would accept that national labour code.

I think a national labour code would remove many of the causes of industrial strife throughout this country such as variations in wages, inequalities in working conditions, and so on. I believe a national labour code would result in a standardization of costs, which would be of great assistance in determining a national standard of living and stabilizing it. Many employers in British Columbia have suggested to me that a national labour code would be of great advantage to those who, in some cases, must compete with industry operating in eastern Canada at lower labour costs. I think it is time that this government gave labour throughout Canada, on a national scale, recognition in line with the increasing responsibility it is asked to accept. That is all I wish to say at this time.

I was interested in the point made by the Minister of Labour about people leaning on the state. Unfortunately in this world it sometimes happens that jt does not particularly matter what we think. As I see it, everything is a process of evolution. and we proceed in conformity with the developments that take place. What is happening. today, not only in Canada but in many other countries-and in the countries that 
developed industrially earlier and faster it has happened before this-is that on the one hand we have large aggregations -of industries, enormously powerful. Because those industries employ large numbers of people, in some cases running into the tens of thousands, those workers brought together in that way organize, first, for their own protection and then, later, for their own advancement. These are conditions over which we have no control. In the struggle between large industries on the one band and large labour organizations on the other, the community would be torn to pieces unless the state stepped in to protect the community. That is the position we are in today, and it is no use trying to wish ourselves out of it because that cannot be done. We must bring to that situation the authority of the state as the protector of the people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

It is a definite result of the progress of industrialization, and we cannot turn back the wheels of progress, even if it were desirable to do so. So we shall have to accept the disadvantages of industrialization along with its benefits, and do the best we can in the circumstances.
I also listened with attention to what was said, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as to the desirability of a national labour code. I think the great majority of the people of this country believe we should have a national labour code. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary West, one of the recommendations of the committee on industrial relations last year approved such a code. But I think I have a very good understanding of what the minister is up against in his efforts to design legislation for that purpose. We are not likely to have a national labour code or, for that matter, many other things that may be desirable in this country as long as certain provinces insist on being sovereign states, and, in my opinion, hold up our progress. What an individual thinks in the matter is not of great importance, because some people would rather be big toads in a little puddle than polliwogs in a big pond. So that is pretty much the position we are in today, and until we learn to discipline ourselves for the common good I suppose there is nothing much we can do about the matter. They have suffered through this sudden change from war to peace, in that a large number of reductions have been made. The result must be obvious, but I am not primarily concerned about that. My concern is over the difficulty the employees at His Majesty's dockyard have experienced in obtaining conditions similar to those which have been authorized for men working in civilian shipyards in the same city and the same area. Is it not possible now to have the union of men working in those dockyards recognized by the dockyard officials? put the facts of that dispute on record time and again. I do not think anyone from the west or from central Canada can render any better judgment on that question in a week's time than can someone who served the people in this dispute for twenty-six years.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is a generous man. I suggest that he should provide the $5 million subsidy immediately so as to get these mines back in operation. Then the government can appoint as many people as it likes during the term of the next contract to go to Nova Scotia and make an examination of the whole set-up, from the point of view of increasing production, and determining who is right and who is wrong in these recurring disputes.
I am prepared to go with them. I will show them the way around, because I konw my way around those collieries. Since I was a member of the committee on industrial relations which sat last year, I should- like to say a. word or two at this time. I am not one who

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PISTOLS, MOTOR CARS, AND PAYMENT OF FINES

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the criminal code (pistols, motor cars and payment of fines).
He said: The bill raises one of the gravest questions we have in this country. I do not apologize for taking up the time of the house at this time, because in the city from which I come over one hundred people were killed and several thousand injured on the roadways alone last year. It- is one of Canada's greatest scandals. Every highway in the country is covered red by the abuse of motor cars by about only five per cent of those who drive. About ninety-five per cent of the people who drive cars are known to be careful.
This matter affects the life and health of the people. As I have said before, I should like to see the criminal code amended and consolidated every ten years like the Bank Act. A legal committee of the house should be appointed to consider the various bills, because when you look at the protection which the public has it is all in the criminal code. There have been numerous changes in the law since the criminal code became part of the revised statutes of Canada in 1906, chapter 146. It is now' contained in the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 36. which supersedes the original code and is the basis of the statute which came into effect on February 1, 1928. There are also changes in the sections iti view of decisions of the privy
Criminal Code

council. There are also some changes in sections 240A and 240B in accordance with 1926 Appeal Cases regarding appeals to the privy council in criminal cases.
In addition, I believe the time has come when this house should have, like the provincial legislatures, a legal committee to consider legal bills, because it is difficult for lawyers, magistrates and judges to know what the law is at the present time. In my opinion the government should take under consideration the question of a judges' committee or a departmental committee to examine, revise and consolidate the provisions of the code pursuant to judgments of the different courts having criminal jurisdiction, and also the suggestions which are made from time to time to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) by bar associations and by police constables' associations and others. The government should provide further that the committee should report its findings to the House of Commons and to the Minister of Justice and, finally, a select committee should be appointed to revise and consolidate the criminal code every ten years. That is my suggestion.
With regard to Bill No. 13, which is a bill to amend the criminal code to deal with pistols, motor cars and payment of fines, I wish to refer to a debate on the second reading of my bill to amend the criminal code (motor cars), which took place before the war. It is all set out in Hansard of February 17, 1938. The debate took all day and all evening. The bill had to do with a proposed amendment respecting the operation of motor cars. I introduced the bill. All leaders of the house spoke on the motion. I said, as reported at page 535 of Hansard:
I wish to call the attention of the house to the great slaughter occurring on our highways. Almost every road is coloured red with the slaughter of men, women and children. This slaughtering is done in a manner that is disgraceful and presents the most important problem with which we have to deal this year. I may say that it is one of Canadas chief problems, and parliament does nothing about it.
We are satisfied to devote a whole lot of time to flag waving, but the government of the day does not seem prepared to sit down and consider what must be done for these helpless men, women and children whose homes have A?iel\Juinec* anc* w*10se liv?s have been wrecked. All this goes on, and yet this high court of parliament sits here and does nothing to deal with these practical problems, which would be a work tor the benefit of the people.
I believe a few facts should be drawn to the attention of the house. The subject of the bill has been discussed in the house for three or four sessions. One of the commandments of God is: Thou shalt do no murder. Many men of real worth, through carelessness and selfishness, are recklessly violating not only the laws of God but those of men. Xo invention has contributed

more to the comfort of our people than has the motor car, hut, like every other invention we must consider its use as one thing and its abuse as another.
During the past century scientific discoveries in medicine, chemistry and physics have resulted in untold good to humanity, but, as in the abuse of inventions, in war they were a curse to mankind.
As I say, nothing has contributed more to the enjoyment and education of the people than the motor car, but when you look at the abuse of it, that is another matter.
Looking into the question one finds invariably a tremendous annual loss from deaths, accidents, injuries and so on. One finds untold sorrow and suffering with intense pain and grief, almost exceeding anything the human imagination could conceive. The suffering brought about by these machines is equalled only by that inflicted by plagues, pestilence, famine, battle, murder and sudden death.
It would be misleading and unfair to attempt to attribute all the blame for these horrors on the highways to all people who drive and use motor cars. The fact is that ninety-five per cent of drivers are trying to obey the law. It is the remaining five per cent about whom I am complaining. They cause the trouble. One has only to see the records to understand the facts. As I study the records of cases I am driven to the conclusion that beyond any doubt the small minority are the major cause of the trouble. They appear to have exploited, for their own pleasure and profit, the generous tolerance of others. They use their cars in an irresponsible, careless and un-Christian way. The fault is grievous, and they can have no ground for complaint if they are put under restraint through application of the criminal code. Ignorance and thoughtlessness are not palliatives. Obedience is the only reparation they can make, and it is long overdue.
I quoted the other evening, in dealing with another bill, the observations of the late able and beloved Chief Justice R. M. Meredith, who was on the supreme court bench for about forty years on circuit in Ontario. He said, when addressing a York county grand jury:
And as now nearly everyone is a ear owner, and car driver, young and old, of all sorts and conditions, it is difficult to get justice in even a civil action. Car-driver jurors have nearly all the speed fever; and self-preservation instincts are so strong that they will not be persuaded to decide against drivers who have been no more unlawful than they themselves often, if not commonly, are.
What then is the remedy? I think it should he: make the laws plain and reasonably severe and enforce them; and cancel licences freely. And at the other end of the matter, give no licence to anyone who is not proved to be mentally and physically, and from experience and knowledge of the highway laws, thoroughly capable.
I continued as follows:
First, we must consider the indifference shown by the five per cent of drivers to the rights and privileges of the people using the highways.

Criminal Code
Then there is the indifference to the convenience of others; there is excessive speed, and congestion. Ever since man has learned to direct a machine more powerful than himself he has asserted his superiority over his neighbour. "Make way or take the consequences" is the cry of the reckless driver. Yet, this indifference is limited to only a small number.
That is the problem. I will not give the figures. They were set out in two reports which were made to the House of Commons last year, tabled for me, showing the number of fatal accidents in Canada at level crossings, on the highways, and1 they ran into the thousands; from drownings, from those who left infants in houses alone and the houses were burnt, from wilful and gross negligence, leaving children three or four years of age alone in the house andi then the house burns down. I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) the throwing of pop bottles on to the ice at hockey games and' all that kind of thing. These things should be under the control of the criminal code, along with many other matters. In this bill I refer to those who go around carrying wooden pistols and frightening girls in candy stores and taking their money. I refer to other cases. One can hardly pick up a newspaper without finding a report of young bandits going around the streets raiding houses and stores, gathering payrolls and all that kind of thing. It is, in my opinion, altogether too easy to get a pistol in Canada. They are not properly registered. If they are registered! many of them are stolen and sold to second-hand stores. There should be a restriction on the carrying of loaded pistols. The very fact that the pistols are loaded would argue that these young people intend to commit some offence, and the carrying of such loaded weapons is very likely to lead1 to a potential murder. The man who carries a loaded weapon is a potential murderer.
Last year, as well as in previous sessions,
I put on Hansard figures showing the number of those killed and injured on our highways as a result of motor car accidents, and I contended then, as I do now, that we should have complete records in this connection. The bureau of statistics has not a modern system so far as records of this kind are concerned. though it is making improvements from year to year. The fact remains, how-« ever, that there is no efficient method of getting at these results. I suggest that we should improve our system and at the same time carry out a campaign of education such as there is in the old country. The figures given by the board of transport commissioners show that in the period between 1940 and
1943	inclusive there were over 2.000 injured and 588 killed at level crossings. The information I have here goes on to discuss drowning and other forms of fatality.
In France, with a population of some 42,000,000 before the war, over 4.000 people were killed by motor cars in one year, though they were spending considerable sums of money in road building.
I may say that I have received many appreciative messages' in support of this bill. I have a telegram dated February 18, 1947, from Mr. Alex Edmison, of the Prisoners John Howard Association, stating that he had received copies of the bill and wishing me every success. He feels that the proposed legislation of time to pay fines as a Summary Offenders Act would be of great benefit in reducing the crime rate in Canada.
I have also a letter from the Reverend John Cobum, secretary of the Canadian Temperance Federation, from which I quote the following paragraph:
I think you will recognize that the police officers are up against an immense task. Magistrates and judges often seem to think that unless a man is drunk he has not committed a violation of the law. As you know of course, this is entirely erroneous. I am told that some states in the union have passed a law making a blood test compulsory on request of a police officer. According to Doctor Rodger's estimate, liquor is killing five people and injuring 84 every week on the highways of Ontario alone. I think if you and a number of the opposition members would let the Prime Minister know you are supporting the government in vigorous action, it will be helpful. Where so many human lives are at stake, this is too important a matter to be a mere party issue. On various occasions you have manifested a spirit of independence in your parliamentary work. I have no doubt whatever, you will do so in this case.
He refers to a brief submitted to the Prime Minister and the government.
To come now to the bill itself, the first section provides that anyone who, without lawful excuse, points a firearm, pistol or airgun, whether loaded or unloaded, is guilty' of an offence. That is an amendment to sections 124 and 126 of the criminal code. Section 2 provides that "pistol" shall include anything in the shape or form and size of a pistol. Section 3 deals with the liability of the driver of a car to stop after an accident.

speechtext:
I want to thank the minister. I have seen the evils of hit-and-run driving. Mr. Speaker. As a former chairman of the police commission in my city, I think this is one of the most important matters that parliament can attend to, and I consider I have done my duty in bringing it to the attention of the house. It is of far greater importance than many of the material things that we have been talking about now for fifty-two days.
The next section of the bill deals with persons driving while under the influence of alcohol or narcotics. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, there is anything more scandalous than the hit and run driver and the drunken driver. I once saw a man drive down an important section of the city of Toronto and knock down two children. One of them was killed instantly and the other badly injured. The Right Hon. Viscount Bennett, on February 17. 1938. in the debate to which I referred, when he was in this house took a strong stand in support of the principle I am now advocating in this bill. He felt that something should be done to meet this grave situation, but nothing has been done since the war started. The casualty list is an appalling one, the number of men, women and children who have been injured in such accidents numbering nearly twice as many as those wounded and killed in the Canadian forces during the same seven years.
There is no doubt that there is some complaint about judges taking cases away from 
juries. In this connection I suggest that hon. members look up the debate that took place in this house on February 17, 1938. As regards persons driving under the influence of alcohol, the present law, I submit, is totally inadequate. When a person is arrested under such circumstances there is considerable doubt, having regard to the decision of the Ontario court of appeal, as to what is a voluntary statement or a free statement made to the police. 1 submit that this should be clearly set out. we should know what is a voluntary, what is a free statement on the part of the accused.
Regarding section 5, hit and run drivers, I suggest that when an accident occurs everyone in charge of a vehicle who is directly or indirectly a party to the accident should remain at the scene of the accident or return immediately and render all possible assistance. Many times such a person kills a. child. The child has just as much right to live as he has; and if it is killed, and the driver runs away, I think it is a most cowardly form of murder. I think it is a terrible thing to see a small child knocked down on the highway, where the driver runs away and nothing is done about the matter. You cannot find him. Sometimes, because of the bad weather you cannot get the number. I believe this is a wise proviso.
With regard to section 7, causing death in a culpably negligent manner, additional penalties are provided. As we saw in this debate in 1938, it takes two people, in a second's lack of attention, to make an accident. If there is one, the person who kills a man should not drive a car for two years where it is found that the accident was largely due to his negligence.
There are only one or two other sections. The one on the trial of young offenders provides that the parents should be notified. I think it is only right that parents of children under age should know when they are charged with an offence and be given a chance to come to their aid, if possible, and that they should be given the protection of the law by the appointment of a lawyer.
The next section has to do with the trial of a female person. This has been up now for ten or twelve years. The suggested amendment in section 9 is:
On the trial of any female person by a jury under any provision of this act, one-third of the furors chosen to try the issue shall be female persons duly qualified on the same basis as male jurors.
A former editor, and a very great editor, the late Mr. Harry Anderson, when this bill was up in 1927 said that women were too temperamental. I do not think they are any more temperamental these days than are

Criminal Code
some of the men. Some of them would make better jurors than men, and I think we would have less trouble with juries making up their minds and coming to a verdict.
Section 10 deals with charge of manslaughter arising out of the operation of motor vehicles, criminal or culpable negligence being proved. It defines the powers of the judge and the powers of the jury. The function of the judge is to explain the law to the jury and the jury is bound to take what the judge says is the law. Questions of fact should be determined by the jury. After all is said and done, what is the way we approach this matter in this country? I have noticed in some of the papers-not all of them-in some cases trial by jury has at times been supplanted by trial by newspaper; that is, in some of the more sensational of our newspapers.
As regards section 11, jury to decide whether guilty or not guilty, on the trial with a jury of persons who cause death or serious injury, it is desirable that the functions of the jury should not be curtailed or abolished. There has been much criticism of many cases of gross negligence having been taken from the jury. The increased number of accidents requires that the law should be brought up to date.
The next section is: fine or penalty in discretion of court. The last clause deals with the law of England regarding fines, known as the Summary Offenders Act. After all is said and done, the gaols of this country are at times full of people who are not able to pay the fines. Why is the fine imposed? In England they are given time to pay the fine. I think it would be a blessing if we could adopt that practice in this country, because we are just back to the days of Dickens in his "Little Dorritt". There is imprisonment for fines for people who have not the money to pay them.
It is for these reasons I thought it wise to bring these matters before the house. I sympathize with and thank the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley). He is one of the most able, hard-working and conscientious ministers we have had in this war and after it. But I think the time has come when we should have a legal committee which should have the proper time to consider these amendments which are most important for the safeguarding of the public. They are all only suggestions for the minister to consider and decide on, as improvements to help lessen loss of life from the motor car.

In order to help the hon. member for Broadview
(Mr. Church) get his bill through the house,
I shall of necessity have to be very brief, and so I shall be. I merely wish to refer to one reference in the bill, namely, motor cars. Like everyone else, I have been interested in the cartoons which have recently appeared in the Globe and Mail in Toronto and which were drawn by one of the most brilliant young cartoonists in Canada. I am told by my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), that Jack Boothe, the cartoonist, comes from his province. If he does, British Columbia lost a capable cartoonist and Ontario gained one. His cartoons every few days are headed "Why People Cannot Grow Old." A few days ago there was one in the paper giving a new angle to motor car accidents, and one I had not seen before. It showed a passenger in a car lighting a cigarette for the driver; of course, the driver was blinded not only by the flame but by the smoke, and an accident took place. That is one cause of accidents. Somebody should be responsible for that.
A few days ago I was standing in front of a building which I happen to own and two men came along to get into a car. Both of them were drunk. They staggered toward the car and, one after the other, tried to get into the car to drive it away. In the end they both got into the car, which meant that one of the drunks drove the car away. I presume the bill which the hon. member for Broadview has in mind would protect the public against the like of that. Certainly anything which this or any other house can do to cut down on deaths from motor car accidents, should be done. What can be done, I do not know. That is a legal problem, and I shall not discuss any of the legal aspects of the bill at all. As a humble member, and as the hon. member for Broadview had put my name down as the seconder of the motion for second reading, I felt that it was my duty to rise and support him. There is no more hard-working member in the House of Commons than the hon. member for Broadview. I have always found him standing aip for the people. In this case he is doing that.
In conclusion, I would just say that during the recent session the Ontario government did take a step in the right direction, if I may say so here, in passing a bill requiring that part of the fee which is paid by the driver for the privilege of driving his car is set aside for the benefit of people who are struck and maimed-in the case of death, of course, to their estates-by those who strike them and run away, hit and run drivers and those who, if caught, are unable to pay anything. I think that is a good step. Somebody should
Criminal Code

pay for the accidents of folks who are not themselves responsible for being struck and who are struck by people who are incapable of paying anything.
With that I shall conclude. I heartily approve my hon. friend's efforts to protect the public from disaster.
