speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we consider the cause of motor accidents I think it is the duty of the government and of all governments in Canada to remove the cause. Yet there are some governments which are stimulating that cause of accidents. Everybody knows that it is very unpopular to say anything about that great cause of motor accidents and destruction in Canada. But if we are sincere in our way of living, we have a right to try to drive out anything which will cause destruction of human life. I think everyone can see what I am driving at. I fear that when the cocktail bars in Ontario are in full swing men and women, young or old, coming home in the small hours of the morning will not have proper control of their automobiles. Therefore I am glad to see in the bill section 4, dealing with those driving while under the influence of alcohol or narcotics. I believe governments should consider this point. If our governments license and receive revenue from anything that causes the destruction of human life, I think they should be big enough to reconsider their position.

speechtext:
I should like to speak briefly on this bill, but first I wish to congratulate the sponsor, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) on having introduced it. The bill contains many commendable features, all of which I do not propose to discuss at this time, but I would particularly mention the reference to driving while under the influence of alcohol or narcotics, hit-and-run drivers, and the liability of a driver to stop after an accident. These matters, I believe, are worthy of careful consideration on the part of this house. Everyone recognizes that many accidents result from faulty judgment on the part of a driver or a pedestrian, while many others result from mechanical deficiencies. We also know, however, that a substantial percentage of accidents are caused by drunken driving. In one medium size Canadian city in which there were fifteen fatal traffic accidents in 1946, three were directly attributed to drunken driving. Perhaps that figure does not sound very large, but it represents twenty per cent of the total; and, no matter what the figure is, it is too high.

This bill is not intended as a cure-all, but as a step in the direction of providing heavier penalties for persons who operate motor vehicles, while under the influence of liquor, and irresponsible drivers, whether or not they be under the influence of liquor. If the provision of stiffer penalties for infractions of the Law will curb the mounting death toll on our highways and the streets of our cities and towns, I think this bill should receive the unanimous approval of the house. I feel sure it will have that effect; therefore I am rising at this time to give it my support. The motor vehicle is a dangerous weapon when operated by an. intoxicated person. It is a murderous weapon when only half controlled by an irresponsible person. Under such management, vehicles are a danger to the public. Infractions of the law by such persons should be met with stiff penalties. Many accidents occur every year on the highways of this country and on the streets of our towns and cities. According to the bureau of statistics, the death toll from motor accidents for the past few years has been as follows:

That makes	a total of	10,893	deaths	duringthe period	this nation	was	at	war,	or	almost

In the same .period more than one hundred thousand people were injured in traffic accidents. These injuries caused the crippling of thousands of people. This was during a period of gasoline rationing, and during a large part of which a speed limit of forty miles an hour was in effect; and the toll is still mounting. The 'latest figures obtainable, which are for 1945, show 1,530 fatal accidents on our highways, or eleven per cent more than in 1944; and from the information already received from the various provinces which report to the bureau of statistics, I fear the figure for 1946 will be substantially higher.
Precautions must be taken against traffic violations, and this parliament has authority to amend the criminal code, which probably is as far as we can go. Of necessity, provincial and municipal governments must complete the task. I believe the amendments offered in this bill will assist local authorities in curbing irresponsible drivers. Acceptance of this bill by the house is the least we can do to meet the growing menace on our highways and on the streets of our towns and cities.

Criminal Code
*In reference to the difficulty which not infrequently confronts the law enforcement authorities in ascertaining whether or not a person apprehended at the scene of an accident is intoxicated, I would suggest that some standard be set up for the guidance of the police. I believe the criminal code should provide that the presence in the blood of an individual of alcohol above a certain percentage should be sufficient reason for declaring the person apprehended to be intoxicated. Local doctors- on whom the police have to rely are often loath to state whether or not a person is in a state of intoxication. With a standard set as a guide, a doctor would only have to state his findings and offer his evidence before the court. I believe such an amendment to the criminal code would be desirable, and it might be opportune to suggest that it be inserted in this bill. In any event I commend the suggestion to the Minister of Justice for his serious consideration.
Motor traffic is certain to increase on our highways during the next few years. Probably thie number of accidents will also increase. The law enforcement bodies should be given every assistance possible to cope with violations of traffic laws, and I feel that the bill as it stands has considerable merit. It will not wholly solve the problem of the increase in the number of accidents, but it will prove of some assistance in curbing irresponsible driving on our congested traffic lanes. Careless drivers endanger not only their own lives but those of innocent people on the roads and streets, who are unfortunate enough all too frequently to be in the way of such drivers. I shall support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think the discussion on the bill has served a useful purpose, and perhaps if the discussion had been a little more extensive it would have been still more desirable.
There is no doubt that the situation which has been described by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and other hon. members is a serious one, and that it is important that the provisions of the criminal code be made as effective as possible. As I said briefly to Your Honour, it is impossible to deal with the bill as a unit because its sections deal with a variety of subjects. It would be awkward to go through the bill, section by section, and to deal with it in that way.
I should like to say, speaking generally about the bill, that there are some sections in it which I think should be incorporated as amendments in the criminal code. Then there
are some sections which I believe should be discarded, for certain reasons which perhaps I shall not give fully to the house at the present time. There are other sections which this parliament should not enact until there has been some consultation with the provinces.
I refer to provisions such as those relating to the constitution of juries, and another one which abrogates a very ancient principle. The suggestion is that a judge should not be permitted to withdraw a case from a jury, even if, in his opinion, there is no evidence to go to the jury.
Those are principles which should not be enacted by parliament, at least, in my opinion, without consultation with the provinces. The government has been giving consideration to the introduction of certain amendments to the criminal code, and a draft bill has been prepared containing a fairly large number of sections. It has not yet received the approval of council, but I anticipate that council will give its approval to a bill containing important amendments to the criminal code. I believe I would not be divulging any confidence if I were to tell the house that some provisions in the bill now before us are substantially the same as some of the provisions in the bill which the government is likely to introduce a little later in the session.
I gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview that, so far as he is concerned, this is not a new bill, and that he has introduced some of these proposals before in the house. I gathered, further, that he felt that previous governments, and possibly this one, had neglected the matter, and that they had not paid very much attention to the suggestions he had made through the years. I hope, when he sees the amendments to the criminal code, he will feel that to some extent he has been repaid for the zeal with which he has sought to remedy those conditions requiring correction.
There are some provisions in this bill which make the penalties much heavier than they now are. When hon. members are giving consideration to the bill I suggest they ought to give some thought to the question as to whether it is desirable to make penalties too heavy. For instance, in this bill there are penalties requiring, in some instances, a minimum imprisonment of six months which, in my judgment, is too stiff. If we were to enact those provisions I believe that, instead of improving the situation, we would make it worse, because it would be much more difficult to get convictions than it is at the present time.
There are sections in the bill which introduce important changes of principle. For
Penitentiary Act

instance, there is the proposal that the offence of driving a motor car while intoxicated should be changed to driving a car while under the influence of alcohol. If that suggestion were to be adopted it would constitute an important amendment. At the present time I am not able to accept it, although I am willing to give consideration to the arguments advanced tonight in favour of the change. However the implications of a change of that kind are far-reaching. It has been urged upon us by delegations, and it is worthy of consideration; but the implications are far-reaching because, if the state of being under the influence of alcohol means that there be just the slightest amount of alcohol in one's system, which I presume to some extent would put a person under the influence of alcohol, then the driving of a car under that condition would become a crime. The house should be careful not to go too far in the creation of crimes.
However I am not prejudging that question. Delegations have made their presentations on the point to the government and the matter is receiving consideration. All I can say is that I am not prepared to accept that principle tonight. It will have to be given some further consideration.
In all the circumstances I suggest that the hon. member permit the bill to stand until the amendments to the criminal code that the government is prepared to sponsor are placed before the house. They will not cover the whole ground. Some of these sections we are not prepared to accept at all; some we are prepared to accept, and some will be accepted in a modified form. But I do not think it is desirable for us to give the bill second reading and go into committee of the whole to deal with the sections one by one, when the whole matter of amendments to the criminal code is receiving consideration and will be dealt with by the house a little later.
Therefore I move the adjournment of the debate.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman moved the adjournment of the debate but, if he does not wish to continue what he was saying, and no one else wishes to say anything I am prepared to go on. This bill contains three sections and is identical with the bill introduced into this house by the hon. gentleman seventeen years ago. One section reads:
The grand jury of any county in which a penitentiary is situated may visit, view and inspect the same, and make such inquiry as to it may seem proper into the state, condition and management thereof, the nature and efficiency of its accommodation, the employment, training and treatment of convicts, the conduct of its officers, prisoners and employees, and of all others having dealings of any kind or in any capacity with such penitentiary, and may examine and inspect the accounts, vouchers, records and books of the penitentiary; and the grand jury may thereupon make such findings and such presentments as it may deem to be required in the public interest.

Emergency Powers
By that provision penitentiaries which are federal institutions would be subject to inspection by grand juries which are provincial bodies. The argument of Mr. Lapointe when he was Minister of Justice was that federal institutions should be subject to inspection by federal officials rather than by provincial officials or provincial bodies and that it would be wrong in principle to have federal institutions inspected by grand juries. That position taken by Mr. Lapointe was probably a sound position, but it seems to me that the stronger reason for opposing the proposal that grand juries be empowered to visit and inspect federal institutions is the illogical nature of the proposal.
There are only two counties in Canada where grand juries would be eligible under this bill to inspect federal institutions. One is the county of Westmorland in New Brunswick where Dorchester penitentiary is situated, and the other is the county of Frontenac in Ontario where two penitentiaries, Kingston penitentiary and Collin's Bay penitentiary, are situated. There seems to be very little reason for delegating to the grand juries of Westmorland county, New' Brunswick, and Frontenac county, Ontario, the responsibility of inspecting these particular federal institutions. There are no grand juries in the province of Quebec or in the western provinces where the other federal institutions are situated, and there is no particular reason why the federal parliament should endow the grand juries of these two districts with this inspectorial function.
It should be borne in mind that grand juries have no particular training in inspeetional work, nor have they any particular knowdedge of criminology or anything of that kind. These facts were pointed out by Mr. Lapointe in the argument he made against this provision in 1930 when he was reported on page 277 of Hansard of March 4, 1930 as follows:
May I point out that such an inspection of a penitentiary as is proposed by this bill would occupy the activities of a grand jury working ten hours a day for several months. May I also mention the fact that the grand juries are composed of excellent men indeed, but they are men with no especial experience in criminology or the handling of criminals, or the management or care of such institutions.

speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock I had called P.C. 946. subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Before the committee rose at six o'clock, the minister deleted six orders in council from the schedule to this bill. I regret that he did not see fit to delete order in council P.C. 946. The purpose of this order, which was first passed in the emergency years of the war, was to deal with the problem of people of Japanese origin. The purpose is clearly stated in paragraph 3 on page 109 of the consolidation. I should like to quote part of that paragraph. It is as follows:
... it is deemed advisable, by reason of the state of war now existing, for the order and welfare of Canada to make provision . . . for the control of persons of the Japanese race in Canada.
During the war years there was justification for that order in council because it was necessary for the government in our war with Japan, to protect Canadians against the possibility of any fifth column activity. Whether there is any justification for it tonight, however, is a different question.
The powers given to the minister by this order in council are widespread. In the first place, it allows the minister virtually to control the lives of all people in this country of Japanese origin. Under it the department may determine where these people have to live. It can determine where these people must work and what wages they are to be paid. At least until recently it determined whether or not they could travel.
Tonight the government is asking parliament to extend for another year these orders in council which control the lives of these people. When parliament is arriving at a decision on this matter there are two facts which should be kept in mind, and I refer them particularly to hon. members from British Columbia. The first of these is the fact that the 1941 census showed that there were approximately 23,000 persons of Japanese origin in this country. Of these 17.200 were
Emergency Powers

Canadian citizens either by birth or by naturalization. Therefore, for the most part, these orders in council are dealing with Canadian citizens. Second, we should remember that when this order in council was passed it was passed as a temporary measure, as an emergency measure needed to expedite the prosecution of the war. I was not here at that time, but I understand from some hon. members who were, that when the order was passed it was intimated that when the emergency war was over, the rights of these people would be returned to them. Today the war is over; it has been over for almost two years; there is no longer any danger of invasion, any danger of insurrection in which these Canadians, even if they wanted to, could play any part, and yet their rights have not been returned to them. Instead, a great many of them are spread across the country living in camps. I am particularly mindful of one group living about four miles south of my own city of Moose Jaw. They are living in an old airport. I do not say that the conditions of these people are intolerable, but certainly, huddled together as they are, their conditions are not good.
As I have said, we are dealing with the rights of Canadians tonight. With the emergency over, I cannot see why the government is asking parliament to extend these powers for another year. It cannot be because these people were disloyal during the war, because despite the way we treated them, despite the way they were uprooted from their homes, despite the way we took their privileges from them, there was not one Japanese Canadian during the war who committed any disloyal act.
When speaking to the house on August 4, 1944, the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 5915 of Hansard:
It is a fact that no person of Japanese race born in Canada has been charged with any act of sabotage or disloyalty during the years of war.
Therefore we cannot be wanting to extend these powers tonight for the reason that these people were disloyal during the war. Nor yet can we say that these people were responsible in anj7 way for the acts of aggression of the Japanese government. They are no more responsible for these acts than any other Canadian. The hon, member for Vancouver East put it aptly a few months ago when he said:
They were not nearly as responsible as the government of this country which insisted on sending war materials to Japan while she was waging war on China.

The government cannot say that they want this power extended for the same reason that they originally passed it, namely, for reasons of defence, because the empire of Japan is prostrated ; it has been conquered; it has been crushed. These Japanese Canadians cannot be any menace. Therefore, why are they denied their rights as Canadians? There is only one answer, andi it has to do solely with racial prejudice and intolerance. These people have committed no crime, nor have they been charged with any. They are denied the privileges of Canadian citizenship; they are persecuted solely because their skin is yellow. Lord Acton, the English historian, once said:
The most certain test by whieb we judge whether a country is really free, is the amount of security enjoyed by minorities.
Today, Mr. Chairman, there is a Canadian minority which is not free; there is a Canadian minority which has no security. The Japanese Canadians are being treated in this country today by methods which are to say the least, akin to some of the methods which were used in German}7 not so long ago.

I do not think I shall answer that. This is a serious matter and is no time for levity. I should like to get on and then the hon. member can go ahead.
Today the government is asking parliament to pass a piece of legislation which gives the minister wide powers. Look at page 110 and you will see the powers of the minister. Under section 2 he can determine the localities in which persons of the Japanese race may reside, and tell them where to live. Under section 4 he may employ persons of the Japanese race for such purposes, at such wages and on such terms and conditions as he may deem advisable. I do not think anyone will say that section 4 is not stringent. He may require any person of the Japanese race, in any place in Canada, to proceed to any other place in Canada. I doubt if there is anyone in this house who can get up tonight and say that if we pass the order in council before us, this Canadian minority will have freedom. Time and again in the house and across the country I have heard members of the Liberal, the Conservative and the Social Credit parties as well as members of our own party decrying the dangers of regimentation and the dangers to personal freedom. Not long ago I heard the hon. member for Lake Centre, in an eloquent speech, make this statement:
I assert that it is a member's responsibility to take a firm stand when he sees freedom being interfered with.
I think that is one of the best statements I have ever heard the hon. member make, and I hope that on this bill, with his usual effectiveness, he will take as firm a stand, in opposition to such an order in council, because this order in council provides for a degree of regimentation which I believe has been unheard of in Canada in peace time. And it is regimentation of Canadians.

It is Canadians that we are talking about, Canadian citizens. We have heard a great deal recently about a bill of
rights, and I think the question before us tonight emphasizes how urgently we need that bill of rights. In the speech from the throne the government intimated that they were going to appoint a committee to study human rights and human freedoms. I hope that such a measure will soon be brought down and will be strong enough to prevent injustices of this kind from continuing. In August, 1944, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking in this house, said, as reported at page 5916 of Hansard:
... it is not to be expected that the government will do other than deal justly with those who are guilty of no crime, or even of any ill intention. For the government to act otherwise would be an acceptance of the standards of our enemies and the negation of the purposes for which we are fighting.
And again:
We must not permit in Canada the hateful doctrine of racialism which is the basis of the nazi system everywhere.
If the Prime Minister were in his seat tonight, I wonder whether he would class this order in council as, in his own words, "dealing justly with those who are guilty of no crime." If he were in his seat, would he say that this order in council is not "the hateful doctrine of racialism" which he so eloquently deplored? I believe that if the Prime Minister were in his seat tonight, he would not approve the passing of this order in council. The charter of the united nations was recently ratified by this parliament and signed by the government. Parliament, in taking that action, pledged this country to respect article 1 of the charter, which guarantees "fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race."
This order in council is based solely on racial discrimination. If parliament passes this order tonight, then Canada is guilty of breaking her word, her pledge to the united nations. Surely the word of the representatives of the people of Canada is more than a scrap of paper. Yet, I do not see how we can pass this order without making it a scrap of paper. Every member, before he votes for the passage of the order in council, should search his conscience. Canada has already needlessly made many of her citizens suffer. Let us not allow this discrimination to continue. I move, therefore, that order in council P.C. 946 as amended be deleted from the bill.

But it was necessary to intern about 700 Japanese in British Columbia because they would not comply with the orders of the government. It is true also that at one time over 10,000 had volunteered to go back to Japan. That was prior to the defeat of Japan. It is also a fact that roughly 4,000 have returned to Japan on a voluntary basis. I hope that by the end of this year the policy of relocation will be completed.
My hon. friend spoke of a section in this order in council having to do with the powers of the minister with regard to hiring. There is an obvious reason for that being in there, in the fact that we had to hire people to work in the relocation centres in British Columbia- people of Japanese race, such as nurses, doctors, dentists and others. As far as my knowledge serves me, the Japanese who were working in this province, in my hon. friend's province and in the other provinces, were working at the prevailing rates of wages.
I sincerely believe that the policy followed by this government in the relocation of these persons of the Japanese race is in their own self-interest and that, if we take the long view, it will be to their great advantage. Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In
what the Minister of Labour said I think he put up rather a bad case for a worse order in council. He tried to transfer the war years to this year of 1947. He knows as well as we do that we are no longer at war; we are no longer under the threat of invasion. Therefore we have to consider these orders in the light of today, not in the light of conditions that existed several years ago. None of us will refuse to admit the danger which existed, but many of us refuse today to admit that the danger still continues.
In the matter of logic I think the minister is quite wrong. There is no one in this country who was not hurt and nauseated when we heard of the atrocities which were committed at Hong Kong, in Japan itself, and in China. But let me point out that atrocities were not committed only by the Japanese. Atrocities were committed by other enemy powers. Therefore, if there is to be logic at all in this order in council we should treat the descendants in Canada of those other enemy nations in exactly the same way that we are treating the Japanese Canadians. If we refuse to do so I say there is no logic in what we are doing, and we are attacking the Japanese purely and simply on racial grounds. This order in council is attempting by compulsion to tell Canadians where they are to live in Canada. It appears that at times the test of loyalty of these Canadians was their willingness to live where the government decided they should reside. Might I read again what has already been read in this house by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, because these words need to be repeated? I refer to the statement by the Prime Minister on August 4, 1944:
Surely it is not expected that the government will do other than deal justly with those who are guilty of no crime, or even of any ill intention. For the government to act otherwise would be an acceptance of the standards of our enemies and the negation of the purposes for which we are fighting.
What do those words mean, if they mean anything? Surely they cannot be used in defence of legislation such as this. Are we dealing justly with people who have been guilty of no crime when we tell them where they must live, when we take from them their

essential civil liberty? I say no; and I think the reason of the house will agree with me. Are we not, in effect, accepting the standards of those enemies whom we fought when we treat a minority in this country in such a way, purely because of racial phobia? In the same speech the Prime Minister went on to say:
Japanese Canadians are persons who have been admitted here to settle and become citizens or who have been born into this free country of ours, and . . . we cannot do less than treat such persons fairly and justly.	,
When we take away their rights, as we have taken them away, those words mean nothing. They are the typical facades which we expect on modem Liberalism. Might I quote also something said by the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of National Health and Welfare and who was then Secretary of State, in a speech to the chamber of commerce of Granby:
For subjects (for citizenship classes) I would take the -whole of this great country-its history,, its peoples, its geography, its resources. I would tell them how fish are caught in the St. Lawrence and how farming is conducted up the Peace river. Throughout I would have one basic theme-faith in Canada and love of Canada.
To those words I say "hear, hear" but only if they mean what they say. I should like the Minister of National Health and Welfare to rise in his place tonight and defend the policy of his government in view of those words, and in view of what he said during the debate last year on the citizenship bill. I must again recall to hon. members that we are not now dealing with a war emergency. Thank heaven we are past that; and as the hon. member for Moose Jaw said, these orders in council are in direct contradiction of the spirit and, indeed, of the words of the united nations charter. These orders in council are based upon racial discrimination, which now has been defined by the international military tribunal as a crime against humanity.
I repeat that in peace time, in normal times, no government has the moral right to decide where any Canadian shall live; and when we permit the government these wide powers the foundations of freedom are being undermined. Hon. gentlemen of the party to my right have been strong proponents of freedom in the last few weeks. Here is a case where freedom is grievously infringed. Then let the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario rise in his place and defend the freedom of the individual in this case. Let the hon. member for Lake Centre get up; let the leader of the official opposition get up and state the position of his party with regard to racial discrimination against minorities in this country. If we permit it against one minority we permit it against

Emergency Powers
every minority. I should like an official declaration of policy from that party which professes to be so sincere in its devotion to liberty.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was just trying to picture the situation that led to the removal of the Japanese from the Pacific coast. subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to correct my hon. friend; it was purely a defensive measure.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I agree with the minister that it was purely a defensive measure. The war being over, we contend that it is time that the restrictions on these people were removed, that they were allowed to take up their rights and privileges as Canadian citizens. That is all we are asking. The Minister of Veterans Affairs has referred to the defence of British Columbia. Surely this country must be in a deplorable state if it is endangered by a few thousand persons of Japanese origin, even if they were all disloyal, and there has been nothing to show that any one of them is disloyal. A few7 old men and old women and children are being kept east of the Rockies or east of the coastal defence zone in order to protect British Columbia from invasion. Surely one has only to consider that contention to see how absolutely weak and senseless it is.
I say that there is a strong sentiment in British Columbia in favour of the removal of these restrictions. I have in hand a copy of a long letter which I am not going to read, which was sent to the Prime Minister of Canada by the Vancouver branch of the Canadian civil liberties union.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friends do not seem to consider this organization very important, but on looking at the letter head I find that the honorary chairman is Doctor G. G. Sedgewick, who is a professor at the university of British Columbia. The chairman is Professor Hunter Lewis, another professor at the university. There is also Doctor S. A. Jennings, vice-chairman, who is another professor at the university. And so on down a long list, most of whom I consider to be good Canadians. Referring to the question of
Emergency Powers

Canadian citizens of Japanese origin, Professor Hunter Lewis had this to say in his letter to the Prime Minister:
They are that, in regard to Canadian citizens of Japanese origin, all federal restrictions imposed on them should be eliminated; the federal franchise should be extended to them; and Canadian citizenship should be restored to those who lost it through being "voluntarily deported".
Since our conclusions regarding these matters are neither partisan, nor lightly nor temporarily held, but are sincere convictions arrived at after serious and lengthy thought, we respectfully ask that you give not only them, but also the arguments supporting them, your full and sympathetic consideration.
1 could read dozens of statements which appeared in the press of British Columbia and in other parts of Canada in support of our position. During the last month we have heard a great deal about restrictions and controls placed on the people of Canada. Outside of the persons mentioned in this older in council there are very few controls of any importance today. But here are controls over the lives and liberties of people who are as much Canadian as you and I. Today there is no reason, defence or any other, why these controls should be continued. As I think of the impositions which have been placed on these people, people who are innocent of the war, innocent of any part in it and innocent of any crime or misdemeanour during the war, I wonder what I might do under simitar circumstances or what the Minister of Labour might do or any member of this committee might do under similar circumstances. They were treated by those who were over them- not all of them, of course-as if they were serfs and the people over them were lords. I have here a letter from a former commissioner of Japanese placement in Vancouver, addressed to a Japanese Canadian who asked permission to visit British Columbia to discuss various matters with those in the relocation camps. The letter is dated June 24, 1946. I have a copy and it reads as follows:
Canada
Department of Labour Japanese Division 360 Homer street,
Vancouver, B.C.
24th June, 1946.
Mr. Kunio Hidaka,
Executive Secretary,
Citizenship Defense Committee,
S06 Jarvis street,
Toronto, Ontario.
Dear Sir:-
We have received your letter of June 20 ask-ink for reconsideration of your request to visit B.C.
We are of the opinion that the best interests are being served of those people of Japanese

origin still residing in our B.C. settlements if arrangements are completed for their relocation at the earliest possible date. We believe that a visit to the settlements for the purpose which you have in mind, would only result in delayed relocation. We believe that such delay is not in the interests of people relocating.
Our regional offices in the eastern provinces have complete information on the descriptions of places and areas to which people may be planning to move, and can easily provide such information on request.
We therefore must adhere to our previous decision in declining to approve the issuance of the necessary permit for you to visit B.C. just at this time.
After all the "our's" and "we's" the letter is signed "T. B. Piekersgill, Commissioner of Japanese Placement." I think it was Mark Twain who at one time said there were three categories of people who could use the plural "we" when referring to themselves. One was a ruling sovereign; the second was the editor of a newspaper, and the third was a person who harboured a tapeworm.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And the fourth was the C.C.F.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Since Mr. Piekersgill is not a ruling sovereign or an editor, I presume he comes in the third category. I refer to that because it shows the attitude which is taken toward these people.
In the United States persons of Japanese origin were also removed from the Pacific coast in much the same way and at the same time as they were removed in Canada. Restrictions have, however, been removed in the United States long ago. All the restrictions that we are discussing here tonight have long ago been removed in the United States. Is there any reason why we should be behind the United States in extending freedom to our citizens? I suggest to hon. members that they consider carefully before they vote down this amendment because, if we do vote it down, we might as well stop talking about liberty.

I am sure that if my hon. friend knew Mr. Piekersgill he would agree with me that he is an efficient civil servant and a decent Canadian. subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
There has been some heat displayed in this debate, particularly by the hon. member for Vancouver East and perhaps by some of this companions in the C.C.F. party. In speaking tonight, I should like to do so quietly and sincerely. I give them credit for speaking sincerely and I think they should give other hon. members of the committee the same credit. Suggestions have been made by the C.C.F. that those who oppose their views are guilty of racial phobia, racial prejudice, intolerance and things of that kind. Surely in the Canadian parliament we can get away from cheap abuse of that kind. It does not help anybody and it is not true. I say that simply to keep the record straight. I mean every word that I am going to say. Perhaps the C.C.F. members will not agree with me but that cannot be helped. I hope that other hon. members of the committee will.
The plan agreed on in opening this debate was that we would deal with five orders in council; in other words, deal with the whole Japanese problem at one time. That was a wise suggestion. These five orders can be divided into four different categories. They cover four different questions. One is the question of whether or not Japanese are to be allowed to fish on the Pacific coast. The second is the question of relocation of the Japanese; whether there should be any restriction on their movements. The third has to do with help to those going back to Japan,
Japanese who asked to be sent back, while the fourth relates to the property of Japanese which is in the possession of the custodian of enemy property.
I start with the last subject first. I think orders in council having to do with the power of the custodian over Japanese property in his possession should be carried on. I do not think there can be much dispute about continuing these orders in council, and in that connection I would say this. In the evacuation there can be little doubt that damage was done to the property of Japanese. No matter how carefully the goods and chattels were handled, there was bound to be damage, and I believe that every member would agree that adequate, in fact generous, compensation should be paid to the Japanese who suffered that damage. Certain steps will be necessary to assess the damage, and I suggest that those steps be taken as quickly as possible and that compensation be paid.
The next subject is assistance to the Japanese who wish to go back to Japan. I have here the figures of the Department of Labour as of March 31, 1947. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but these figures show that to that date 3,961 Japanese had been repatriated. The adults in that group asked to be sent back to Japan; they were not sent against their will but insisted upon being sent back. Anyone over sixteen years of age had to sign a request for repatriation and of course that very act showed where their loyalties were.
I do not think it can be successfully argued now that any of these people had a first loyalty to Canada. Their first loyalty was to Japan and they have been sent back. I understand that others still in Canada have asked for repatriation, that there are some now waiting to be repatriated, and it is expected there will be quite a few more when the hostels now in operation are closed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If these people had not been moved from the Pacific coast and put in camps with all their rights and privileges taken away, does the hon. member think they would have asked to go back to Japan?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In my opinion they would have gone. We have always known that among Japanese on the Pacific coast there was an intense loyalty to Japan. At the time the registration was made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police before Japan struck, it was found that there were 1,500 children of Japanese in Canada actually over in Japan at the time. They were going over there in many cases to take military training. They could never cease to be subjects of Japan, and to a
Emergency Powers

degree they were to be admired for the stand which they took. They insisted on being Japanese, but doing so made it very difficult for them to become Canadians. That is a fact which hon. members must face. I have here a clipping from tonight's Ottawa Citizen, which I quote:
Canadian-Born Jap Sentenced to death. Hong Kong, April 22-(Reuters)	Kanao
Inouye, 30-year-old Kamloops, B.C. born Japanese, today was sentenced to death by the Hong Kong supreme court which convicted him of high treason.
Inouye left Canada for Japan in 1935 for university education and military service but said shortly after the war he still was a British subject.
He was remembered well by Canadian prisoners of war captured at Hong Kong in December, 1941, and was accused of ill-treating them on many occasions.
When he appeared before a war crimes court he escaped several charges by pleading he was a British subject. Then he reversed his defence when he came up on the treason charges, saying he had always regarded himself as a Japanese.
But Chief Justice Sir Henry Blackall said Inouye was a natural-born British subject and had remained,so at all times.
Another feature to be considered in connection with loyalties is that there were over 700 male Japanese interned at one time during the war. When you consider that the total population of Japanese, male and female, adult and children, was about 23,000 and that over 700 were interned, that is a very high percentage of the adult males, and yet it was necessary to intern that number.
My friends of the C.C.F. always make a great point of there having been no sabotage. Usually sabotage does not occur until the right time. These people were moved off the coast and over 700 were interned; the Japanese never actually landed, and I suggest to hon. members that these facts do not warrant anyone saying that there would not have been sabotage had the opportunity arisen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And they were probably under instructions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member has brought forward certain cases of disloyalty in the last war. There was another war. Has he any figures in regard to the attitude of Canadian citizens of Japanese origin during the war of 1914-1918?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
They were our allies then, and quite a few Japanese Canadians served with the Canadian forces and served with great distinction. That is very7 much to their credit.
With regard to assistance in sending back those who wish to go to Japan, I think the government is wise in carrying out that policy and I hope the assistance will be forthcoming in the future for those who want to go.

To come now to fishing, and I really think this is the main question when we are dealing with the Japanese. When the Japanese first came to British Columbia I do not quite remember, although I was born in that province, but it was about the time I arrived; well, over fifty years ago-about fifty years ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: More or less.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The Japanese who came were largely fishermen, and it was not many years until it was quite evident that there was grave danger that they would take over the whole fishing industry. There was friction between the Indians and whites and the Japanese. The Japanese were very aggressive, and, as I say, it was not long until there was grave danger that they would control the industry. So that eventually a policy was adopted by the Canadian government of cutting, down the number of fishing licences issued to Japanese. I have here the report of the fisheries branch of the department of marine and fisheries for 19251926. At that time the Right Hon, W. L. Mackenzie King was Prime Minister of Canada and our late friend, the Hon. Mr. Cardin, was minister of marine and fisheries. At page 53 of that report we find this statement under the heading "Reduction in Orientals":
The department's policy of eliminating the oriental from the fisheries of the province with a view to placing the entire industry in the hands of white British subjects and Canadian Indians appears to be working out well as is shown by statement No. 10, which covers a very large proportion of the total number of licences issued which orientals were permitted to hold. In the salmon gill-net operations the orientals during the year 1925 held only 24 per cent and in the salmon trolling 10-5 per cent of the total number issued in the province.
In the herring dry salting operations a further reduction of 25 per cent was made during the year, making a total of 50 per cent, and in the case of salmon dry salting a first reduction of 25 per cent went into effect and it is the intention to continue this percentage each year until these industries are entirely in the hands of whites or Canadian Indians.
That was the policy twenty years ago and more. I have never heard the members of the C.C.F. or any other members from British Columbia protest against that policy until today when we have the hon. member for Vancouver East saying that he wants the Japanese to go back into the fishing business on our coast.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

licences numbered 2,095, apparently. The first thing that was done when the Japanese struck was to call in every one of those fishing boats. Every Japanese fishing boat was called in at once. It was a very wise move and it was a 83166-149
move that was not questioned by anybody in British Columbia. I have never yet heard anybody in British Columbia question the wisdom of that move.

And also, I have never
heard anybody question the evacuation of the Japanese from the coast. I have here a wire which was sent out from Vancouver on February 24, 1942, to all the British Columbia members and, I take it, to the Prime Minister. It reads as follows:
Owing to widespread public alarm over enemy aliens on the Pacific coast and especially respecting those astride vital defence points and with a view to stabilizing public opinion and in the interest of public safety the undersigned met and now urge-
1.	That military authorities be immediately authorized to remove enemy aliens from any and all points considered by military authorities essential in the interests of proper and adequate defence and public safety.
2.	That the evacuation of all those of Japanese origin from the Pacific coast area be proceeded with immediately and plans to this effect announced.
And that is signed by whom, do you think? It is signed by:
M. C. Robinson, chairman; Austin C. Taylor; J. H. Roaf; J. A. Clark; B. 0. Moxon; J. P. Fell; B. Showier-

In February, 1942, he said:
Nobody needs to be a secret service agent to know that a Japanese fifth column will work wherever the Japanese government wants it to work. It is not a question of the loyalty or disloyalty of individual Japanese, native born or otherwise. In a total population of some
25,000	there is no conceivable way of keeping the Japanese government from planting or employing active fifth columnists to do whatever it wants done.
The entire Japanese population should be moved from this coast as soon as it is humanly possible. That means now-before an actual military action can take place.
But to get back to the boats: Many of the boats which were taken in were high-powered ones. I have spoken to men who inspected them, and they said it was amazing to find these boats which could go right across the Pacific. They were not ordinary fishing boats at all, but were boats with great power. I do not think there is anyone in British Columbia who will question the fact that Japanese naval men were trained in fishing boats on the Canadian coast. That was done on every other coast where they landed, and a person would be childish to think it was not also done on our own coast.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can the hon. member state for a fact that it was done on the coast?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

That would not be
accepted in a court of law. My hon. friend is a lawyer, and he knows very well that what he is saying would not be taken in a court of law.
[.Mr. Green.]

speechtext:
The court might take
judicial notice.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think either that there can be any question that had Japanese troops landed on the Pacific coast they w'ould have obtained great help from at least some of the Japanese who were there at the time. There would have been a great many unpleasant happenings such as occurred in Nanking, Singapore and everywhere else they went. I must urge that the people of the Pacific coast are entitled to protection from such a situation ever arising again. I do not think Canadians in other parts of the country have the right to expect Canadians on the Pacific coast to face the possibility of such happenings ten years from now or even a hundred years from now. We were nearly caught once; let us not get into a position where we can be caught again. I have great faith in the common sense of the members of this house, and I believe the great majority will agree that my request is reasonable.
The Japanese are now out of the fishing on the coast, and that policy should be maintained. Of course this order in council is to be continued only for a year, with the possibility of the bill being extended for another year. I suggest that, as far as fishing is concerned, it should be made the permanent policy, and not a matter of only a short time; that the policy laid down twenty or twenty-five years ago should not be dropped at this time.
Finally, to come to the question of relocation, as I understand the government policy -and again I would ask the Minister of Labour to correct me if I am wrong-it is one of dispersal and resettlement. To get the Japanese dispersed is only part of the solution; they also have to be resettled, and I am afraid that part of the policy is far from complete. One reason I say that is that on March 31 of this year there were still 6,618 Japanese in British Columbia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is east of the Rockies?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No; that is in British Columbia west of the Rockies. That is about one in three, and is far greater than the proportion of Japanese we should have if they are to be dispersed on the basis of population. I am afraid what has been happening is that many of what I might call the more stubborn and scheming Japanese have refused to come east. Japanese have never been forced to come east at any time; they have been persuaded by the government to do so. I think the tough ones have remained in the interior

Emergency Powers
of British Columbia, with the idea that as soon as the protected zone is removed they will simply move back to the coast. The result, of course, would be that those who have not been playing the game with the government would get the benefit, while those who accepted the removal and came back east and tried to get resettled will be landed back here in the east, and the others back on the coast will be laughing at them. I think that is the position; the tough ones are just refusing to move from British Columbia; they are just staying there waiting until they can get back to the coast. That impression is verified by a statement made by a Japanese spokesman in Alberta on September 10, according to a clipping of the same date from the Vancouver Province headed "3,500 Japanese evacuees eager to return to coast." It is a dispatch from Raymond, Alberta:
"Nearly every last one of the 3,500 Japanese evacuees in southern Alberta would rush back to the coast immediately if authorities permitted us to return to British Columbia."
That was the opinion expressed by a spokesman here for the Japanese as he described "the almost desperate anxiety" of his fellow countrymen to be permitted to return to their former places of residence and employment.
"Most of us have been in southern Alberta for more than four and a half years now and have helped raise five crops of sugar beets," the former operator of a small store in Vancouver explained. "But we have not become accustomed to this part of Canada or to the kind of work we must do. We would like to go back to the coast, where the climate is better and where we might be able to return to our former occupations."
Another reason I say the policy is not yet complete is that very few are moving east of the Rockies now. On the minister's own figures I find that only 132 moved east of the Rockies between January 31 and March 31.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You would not expect them to move at this time of year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I must admit that I do not want to move here myself in the winter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would not want to move into Saskatchewan or Ontario, for that matter, in January, February or March.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Then I have a statement by the premier of Alberta on February 12 of this year, at Edmonton, in which he is quoted as follows;
Premier Manning said Tuesday the Alberta government has reminded the dominion government several times since the end of the war of the agreement that Japanese placed in this province after their evacuation from the Pacific coast would be removed.
83166-149J
So not only are the Japanese in Alberta anxious to move; the Alberta government is insisting that the dominion carry out its agreement with the province, which was that the Japanese relocated there would be removed at the end of the war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Did they suggest where they might be moved?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, not yet. Then I have the opinion of the deputy minister of labour in regard to the present position of this dispersal policy. I am quoting from The New Canadian, published by the Japanese, dated February 8, 1947. It is a very interesting paper. The heading is: "May Seek Control of Evacuee Movement for Two Years". The dispatch reads:
Ottawa.-Special legislation which would give the Department of Labour power to control the movement of Japanese in Canada for at least two years more may be sought from parliament this session, it was indicated here February 4 by Arthur MacNamara, deputy minister of labour.
Mr. MacNamara said that such legislation might be sought in an effort to prevent a general movement of Japanese back to the province of British Columbia where the bulk of Japanese lived prior to Pearl Harbor.
"Our hope is that the Japanese who are spread throughout the east and west will settle down where they now are. However, it will take time to get them satisfactorily settled and merged into the economy of the other provinces," he pointed out.
"In this respect we feel that we should have control over their movements for at least two years more."
Personally I believe that the government can prevent congestion only by maintaining the whole of British Columbia as a protected zone; not only the coastal area, because that would be unfair to the interior of the province, but the whole of British Columbia. That would mean some Japanese would be there by permit, but there would be control over the movement. So I ask that the protected area be maintained. One year will certainly not ensure either dispersal or resettlement. I appeal to the committee to give consideration to these facts, and if they do so I am sure they will support the pleas of all the members from British Columbia with the exception of the hon. member for Vancouver East, and perhaps the other C.C.F. members wh-o have not said "boo" about this matter yet.
Finally, there is one other feature of the Japanese question, and that is the matter of future immigration. It does not come directly under these orders in council, but I would remind members of the government that on August 4, 1944, the Prime Minister said:
.	. the government is of the view that,
having regard to the strong feeling that ha*
Emergency Powers

been aroused against the Japanese during the war and to the extreme difficulty of assimilating Japanese persons in Canada, immigration of Japanese into this country should not be allowed after the war. It is realized, of course, that no declaration of this type can or should be attempted which would be binding indefinitely into the future. Nevertheless, as a guiding principle in the years after the war, it is felt that the migration of Japanese should not be permitted.
The question of the immigration of orientals is up this year. I do hope the government will keep in mind the statement of policy on Japanese immigration which was announced by the Prime Minister on August 4, three years ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As a member from the interior of British Columbia, and after what has been said this evening by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the hon. member for Vancouver South, I should like to add a few *words in order that the committee may have the right perspective in the situation.
I admit, in the first place, that in the coastal areas there is a considerable body of opinion which is opposed to the return of the Japanese. But I think, at the same time, a great deal of that opinion has been artifical'ly stimulated by speeches such as we hear in the house.
Before going farther, I wish to say this in fairness to the government and to the Minister of Labour that, under the circumstances, and speaking generally, I believe the government did a fair and reasonable job in handling the Japanese situation. In view of the hysteria and the pressure from within their own ranks, I think they were reasonably fair and decent about the matter.
But I rise tonight to support the point of view which has been advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I do so in the first instance, because I come from a riding in which there were large numbers of Japanese residing during the war, after the evacuation from the coast.
During my election campaign I made clear where I stood on the question of race, creed and colour. I ran my campaign on the basis of the principles set out in the Regina manifesto, and I do not intend to desert those principles, even if I lose every vote in my constituency at the next election.
As hon. members know, the Regina manifesto was opposed to any discrimination as to race, colour or creed. That is the fundamental basis of the attitude of the C.C.F. I believe the C.C.F. group in Canada is the only movement which has consistently adopted that attitude throughout these difficult years.

The question of the removal of the Japanese from the coast was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver South. He read a telegram in that connection, in which were included members of several parties, including representatives of the legislature. Everyone knows that in British Columbia all parties supported the removal of the Japanese from the coast at that time. One must view the situation differently today from what he did at that time. Then we had an emergency situation, a situation in which there was some hysteria and a great deal of concern regarding the defence of our coast. We cannot justify our peacetime action on the basis of what we do under the urgent necessities of war.
Before going farther, may I say that not only because I believe in the principles of the Regina manifesto, but because I believe in the principles that Canada has supported in the united nations charter, I support the proposal made by the previous speakers.
I served in the first great war for three years, and I remember that on many occasions chaps like myself had discussions. That war was, in some respects, more bloody and more costly in loss of infantry than was the one through which we have just passed. The Canadian troops in the first great war suffered some ghastly experiences.
I remember one occasion when, along with some others, we captured a trench, and occupied it. To be specific, it was Regina trench, on the Somme. At that time we captured a German officer. Then we had to clear up the trench, and bandage the officer. That was the first time I began seriously to consider this question. We sat in that trench for the remainder of the night-that wounded German officer, along with wounded Canadians and others who were not wounded-discussing this whole situation. All of that small group of men that night decided that, whatever happened in the future, they would do what they could to prevent the recurrence of such a disaster to mankind.
After the first great war, along with many others I heartily supported the league of nations. We saw its ghastly failure, not through lack of interest of the little man or the common people, but through betrayal of those at the top. We have now gone through another war, and this time the united nations organization has been set up. Under it, certain principles have been established, and Canada has confirmed and endorsed those principles.
Now, right in this House of Commons tonight, we hear the Minister of Veterans

Emergency Powers
Affairs rationalize or try to justify-and he is a minister of the cabinet-a desertion of those very principles, and at this early stage.
Canada is pledged to the principles of the united nations, including article 55, paragraph (c) of which reads:
Universal respect for, and observance of, human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.
Because we have pledged ourselves to that, I take the stand as I do tonight, with other hon. members who have spoken. After listening to the Minister of Veterans Affairs rationalizing his point of view toward the charter of the united nations, and his attitude toward the Japanese situation, I would presume that that is what he would call a compensated argument.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I ask a question? What about paragraph 7 of article 2 which reads:
Nothing contained in the present charter shall authorize the united nations to intervene in matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state or shall require the members to submit such matters to settlement under the present charter; but this principle shall not prejudice the application of enforcement measures under chapter VII.
This last chapter, as the hon. member knows, applies only to war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In answer to that, I would say that the whole spirit of the principles of the united nations would indicate that questions of race, colour and creed were international questions, and not national questions within the confines of a nation itself.
We have heard the argument advanced which would indicate that the great majority of people in the coastal part of British Columbia are opposed to the. return of the Japanese. I shall try to be as brief as possible, but in that connection I would quote from the Vancouver Daily Province of February 21, 1946. I shall quote only a portion of the editorial, but would ask hon. members to bear in mind that daily papers are not in the habit of publishing unpopular editorials.
This deals with the Japanese situation. It is a newspaper which, I believe, supports hon. members to my extreme right, and it has this to say when dealing with the Japanese question:
There are certain rights which are vital and fundamental. They should not be subject to revocation or destruction or interference. They should be sacred. Citizenship is one of these rights. The people of the United States long ago, saw to it that their fundamental rights were safeguarded. They placed a Bill of Rights in their constitution, and no president, no state or federal administration, no congress or court can interfere with them.
Wc have no such Bill of Rights in Canada, and incidents have arisen repeatedly in the past fen years to show that we should have one. There was the padlock law in Quebec. There was the attempt of the Alberta government to destroy the freedom of the press. There was the bid of the present federal government only a few months ago for unheard-of powers under the Emergency Powers Act. And now there is this judgment.
Seven hundred thousand Canadians fought recently to protect fundamental rights. Tens of thousands laid down their lives. Are we going, now, to allow these fundamental rights to go by default? Or are we going to do something to guarantee them?
That is whj- I take the position I have taken tonight. I believe it is time we did something about guaranteeing them, and this is a step in the right direction.
The hon. member for Vancouver South I believe was born in a small city in my constituency, the city of Kaslo. Unless I am misinformed, when the matter of bringing the Japanese into the interior was first mooted the hon. member for Vancouver South used every effort to prevent the Japanese from being sent to Kaslo. The hon. member will correct me if I am wrong in my statement. That was dbne because it was stated to be in opposition to the wishes of the residents of Kaslo.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Some of the people wanted them, the merchants for example, because of the business that would be done; the legion did not want them, it was about fifty-fifty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is the point I was about to make. As in other small districts, there was a minority opposition, and that opposition was based upon what they had read in certain papers and what had been said by certain gentlemen. After they came to know these people better, after they had cooperated with them they began to understand them. I can understand that because of what happened in my own small unincorporated village of some 750 people. There was a minority opposition to their coming to that place but, after they had worked in various households, in the mills and on the farms-quite a number of farmers took them -and after some of them joined the Canadian Legion, that attitude changed and it has largely disappeared. I should like to read an editorial from the Kootenaian published in Kaslo, B.C. Weekly newspapers are not in the habit of publishing editorials which are against the general opinion of their subscribers, because most weekly papers published in small districts exist on a very narrow margin. If it were not for advertising and things of that sort they
Emergency Powers

could not exist. This is what was said in the Kootenaian of December 27, 1945, when the movement first commenced:
No wholesale deportation of our Canadian J apanese
We have lived with our Canadian Japanese in Kaslo for nearly four years, and we have seen them maintain their homes calmly under conditions that would have been the subject of much protest by any of the rest of us. We have watched neat, well groomed school children emerge daily from cramped, crowded family quarters, and we have noted the respect and companionship of our own school students for their Japanese classmates. We have worked in the same shop with a group of Japanese Canadian men, and have noted how naturally many of these have fitted into the business, industrial and athletic life of our city. We have seen professional and university trained men and women submit patiently to extraordinary restrictions in the war-time emergency just passed. We have noted the difference between the federal government's dispersal attitude toward our Japanese (as enunciated by Premier King in September of 1944), and the apparent total deportation policy of the coast men, entrusted by Ottawa with the handling of Japanese affairs in B.C. We have heard otherwise sane white residents of Victoria and Vancouver declare that every Jap should be driven out of Canada by force. And we have also read that excellent, fair and unanswerable letter which appeared in a recent issue of the Nelson News, where a Christian citizen, without bias in one direction or the other, points out our obvious duty as Canadians to fight any such Hitlerian action in corn lection with our Japanese, or any other racial minority.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware of the fact that the editor was one of those who urged that the Japanese be brought in?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am quite aware of that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And he came from the prairies.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I might say that this editor is a Liberal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With a small "1"?

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
With a small "1" as well. The editorial continues:
We review the issues which precipitated the war just over in Europe, and we wonder if these race haters actually think they can get away with such sectionalism in our young Canadian democracy. We look across the line to U.S., and note the comparative fairness of treatment of American Japanese, many of whom have been given full citizenship privileges, and all of whom were given an opportunity to enlist and to fight for the country of their adoption.
We note all these things, and many more, and we have decided that the anti-Japanese party in B.C. have never learned to view this as a national problem; their experience with Japanese competition, and their resultant dislike, has clouded their national vision. fMr. HerridgeJ
The Canadian Japanese are ready to fight for their rights, and no less an authority than the Winnipeg Free Press sums up an editorial championing their fight against deportation, in the following paragraph:
"Neither the naturalization nor the immigration acts would appear to permit a general indictment to be made against Canadian citizens of Japanese birth, or even Japanese nationals resident in Canada. Each man, unless willing to go, must be tried and pronounced unfit to remain in this country."
Well informed Japanese Canadians have long since decided that their future as Canadian citizens depends on a dispersal throughout Canada. And the federal government should assign so many to each of the provinces with B.C. of course taking her quota! We firmly believe that their industry, thrift, cleanliness and adaptability will quickly win them friends wherever they go, and as a result our Japanese problem would solve itself.
I have had letters from people of all political faiths. I have received letters from dozens and dozens of members of the Progressive Conservative party in my riding, some of which expressed disappointment at the attitude taken by many of their own members. I have had letters from members of the Liberal party and from members of church groups, labour groups and from many other people. The point of view expressed by some hon. members is not a fair presentation of the situation. In the coastal region there are substantial. numbers who are opposed to the return of the Japanese, but I would say that a great majority of the people in the interior would like to see the Japanese treated as Canadian citizens.
I wish to quote one or two authorities tc hon. members opposite, particularly the Minister of Veterans Affairs who is so oratorical when it comes to the principles of Liberalism.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have never deserted them, as my hon. friend did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I never deserted the real principles of liberalism, with a small "1". The first authority I should like to quote from is, "Liberalism. Its .principles and proposals." By Herbert Samuel, one of the great authorities of the Liberal party in Great Britain. I do not think anyone will question the authority of so prominent a Liberal. He has this to say on an issue like this:
That it is the duty of the state to secure to all its members, and all others whom it can influence, the fullest possible opportunity to lead the best life.
And again:
The trunk of the tree of Liberalism is rooted in the soil of ethics.

Questions
The next authority is, "Liberalism" by L. T. Hobhouse, and I quote:
So far as elementary rights are concerned there can be no question as to the attitude of Liberalism.
It stands for the freedom of the subject.
In conclusion, I appeal to the .government and to hon. members opposite to return to the principles of Liberalism. I appeal to them to be liberal in every sense of the word and give these people justice, give these people their rights. During the whole debate this evening the face of the Minister of Labour has been beet red and I am sure he has been uncomfortable.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The speech my hon. friend is making would not turn any man's face red; it would turn it green.

subtopic: CONTINUATION' OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My speech was not the occasion of the minister's face turning red; it has been red since nine o'clock. I ask the members of the government'-and there are a lot of men on the opposite benches who think differently from some of the members from British Columbia-to consider this problem from the point of view of the Liberal principles which they profess.
Progress reported.
It being three minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
